lessons.title: 1. Hola: greetings and goodbyes
lessons.subtitle: Buenos días, ¿qué tal?, hasta luego

explanations.title: Hello, at any hour
explanations.body:
Hola works at any time of day, with anyone you would say “hi” to. To match the hour, or to sound a little more polite, use buenos días (good morning, until about midday), buenas tardes (from lunch until dark) and buenas noches (the evening, and also “good night” when you leave or go to bed).

All three are plural: Spanish wishes you “good days”, not “a good day”. Tap a row to hear it.

explanations.title: How are you?
explanations.body: Spanish has two ways of saying “you” to one person. Tú is for friends, family, classmates and children; usted is for strangers, older people and anyone you want to treat with respect. The question changes with it, and so does the little question you send back.

tables.note: ¿Y usted? and ¿Y tú? mean “and you?”. Sending the question back is polite in any language.

examples.text: Muy bien, gracias.
examples.translation: Very well, thank you.

examples.text: Bien, gracias.
examples.translation: Fine, thanks.

examples.text: Regular.
examples.translation: So-so.

examples.text: No muy bien.
examples.translation: Not so good.

explanations.title: Goodbye
explanations.body: Hasta means “until”, so most goodbyes name the time you expect to meet again. Adiós is the plain goodbye and can sound final; hasta luego is the everyday one.

exercises.prompt: It is five in the afternoon and you meet your teacher in the street. What do you say?
exercises.explanation: Tardes means “afternoons”. After lunch and before dark, it is buenas tardes.

exercises.prompt: It is eight in the morning and you meet a friend. Which greeting fits?
exercises.explanation: Morning is buenos días. ¿Qué tal? is a casual question, fine with a friend.

exercises.prompt: Buenas ___, profesor. Ya es muy tarde.
exercises.explanation: The sentence says it is already very late. In the evening, buenas noches.
exercises.promptTranslation: Good evening, professor. It is already very late.

exercises.prompt: Which question is polite enough for an older stranger?
exercises.explanation: Usted marks respect, and the verb form está goes with it. The other three are informal.

exercises.prompt: Your friend asks “¿Cómo estás?”. Which reply means “So-so”?
exercises.explanation: Regular is “so-so”. Muy bien is “very well”, and nada nuevo means “nothing new”.

exercises.prompt: You are leaving class and will see your teacher tomorrow. What do you say?
— ¿Cómo está usted? — Muy bien, gracias. ¿Y ___?
exercises.explanation: You sent the formal question, so you send back the formal “and you?”: ¿Y usted?
exercises.promptTranslation: — How are you? — Very well, thank you. And you?

exercises.prompt: Which of these is NOT a goodbye?
exercises.explanation: ¿Qué tal? is a greeting (“how’s it going?”). The others all end a conversation.

exercises.prompt: Why are buenos días and buenas tardes plural?
options: Because they are only used in writing.
Spanish wishes you “good days” and “good afternoons”.
exercises.explanation: The plural is part of the fixed expression, whoever you are talking to.

lessons.title: 2. Me llamo…: names and introductions
lessons.subtitle: ¿Cómo te llamas? Mucho gusto

explanations.title: What is your name?
explanations.body: To ask someone’s name you use the verb llamarse, which literally means “to call oneself”. You will meet its full conjugation later; for now learn the three phrases as units. The question again depends on tú or usted.

tables.note: Me llamo = “I am called”. Se llama = “he, she is called”.

examples.text: Me llamo Daniel.
examples.translation: My name is Daniel.

examples.text: ¿Cómo se llama su profesora?
examples.translation: What is your teacher’s name?

examples.text: Mi amigo se llama Hugo.
examples.translation: My friend’s name is Hugo.

explanations.title: Pleased to meet you
explanations.body: After the names, say mucho gusto (“much pleasure”). A man can say encantado, a woman encantada: the word describes you, so it agrees with your gender. The other person answers igualmente (“likewise”) or mucho gusto too.

examples.text: Me llamo Lucía. Mucho gusto.
examples.translation: I’m Lucía. Pleased to meet you.

examples.text: Encantada, señor Vargas.
examples.translation: Delighted, Mr. Vargas. (a woman speaking)

explanations.title: Señor, señora, señorita
explanations.body:
Use señor (Mr.), señora (Mrs.) and señorita (Miss) with a family name, to be polite. In writing they are shortened to Sr., Sra. and Srta.

Spanish names usually have two family names. A child takes the father’s first surname and then the mother’s first surname: Marta Ruiz Vega is the daughter of Pablo Ruiz Lara and Elena Vega Ortiz. A married woman normally keeps her own name instead of dropping it.

examples.text: Buenos días, señora Ramos.
examples.translation: Good morning, Mrs. Ramos.

examples.text: Buenas tardes, señor Vargas.
examples.translation: Good afternoon, Mr. Vargas.

examples.text: Me llamo Ana López Ruiz.
examples.translation: My name is Ana López Ruiz.

exercises.prompt: You meet a classmate and want to ask her name informally. What do you say?
exercises.explanation: Te llamas goes with tú. Se llama usted is for the formal “you”.

exercises.prompt: You are speaking to an older man you do not know. Which question asks his name?
— ¿Cómo te llamas? — ___ Elena.
exercises.explanation: You are talking about yourself, so Me llamo (“I am called”).
exercises.promptTranslation: — What’s your name? — My name is Elena.

exercises.prompt: Mi hermano ___ Jorge.
exercises.explanation: Se llama = “he is called”. Me llamo is only for “I”.
exercises.promptTranslation: My brother’s name is Jorge.

exercises.prompt: A woman has just been introduced to someone. What should she say?
exercises.explanation: Encantado/a describes the speaker, so a woman says encantada.

exercises.prompt: Someone says “Mucho gusto.” Which reply fits?
Pablo Ruiz Lara and Elena Vega Ortiz have a daughter, Marta. What is her full name?
exercises.explanation: First surname of the father (Ruiz), then first surname of the mother (Vega).

exercises.prompt: What does “Buenos días, señora Ramos” show?
options: A greeting to a close friend.
A polite greeting with a title and a family name.
exercises.explanation: Señora + surname is the respectful way to greet a woman.

lessons.title: 3. Writing Spanish
lessons.subtitle: ¿ ¡ ñ, accents, and letters that mislead

explanations.title: Punctuation: two marks for every question
explanations.body: Spanish opens a question with ¿ and closes it with ?. An exclamation opens with ¡ and closes with !. The opening mark goes where the question or exclamation begins, which may be in the middle of a sentence.

examples.text: ¿Cómo te llamas?
examples.translation: What is your name?

examples.text: ¡Hola, Marta!
examples.translation: Hi, Marta!

examples.text: Marta, ¿cómo estás?
examples.translation: Marta, how are you?

explanations.title: Accent marks
explanations.body:
A written accent (tilde) is not decoration. It marks a stressed syllable that the usual rule would not predict. The rule: a word ending in a vowel, -n or -s is stressed on the next-to-last syllable (HA-blo, HA-blan, CA-sas); any other word is stressed on the last syllable (ha-BLAR, ciu-DAD). When a word breaks the rule, it gets a mark.

Accents also separate words that sound the same, and every question word carries one.

rows: ends in a vowel but stress is last
ends in -n but stress is last
ends in -z but stress is first

explanations.title: Letters that mislead an English speaker
explanations.body:
Ñ is its own letter, like “ny” in canyon (mañana). H is always silent (hola sounds like “ola”). J sounds like a strong English h (trabajo). V and b are pronounced the same. LL sounds like y in yes in most places (llamo). Q is always followed by u, and the u is silent (que, quien).

Days, months, languages and nationalities are written with a small letter (lunes, español, mexicana), and yo (“I”) is never capitalised.

exercises.prompt: Which is the correct way to write “How are you?”
exercises.explanation: Spanish questions open with ¿ and close with ?.

exercises.prompt: Which is correct?
exercises.explanation: An exclamation needs both marks: ¡ at the start and ! at the end.

exercises.prompt: In “Marta, ¿cómo estás?”, why does the ¿ come after the name?
options: The question starts after the name.
exercises.explanation: The opening mark sits where the question begins, even in the middle of a line.

exercises.prompt: Which word needs a written accent?
exercises.explanation: It ends in -n but is stressed on the last syllable, which the rule would not predict.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence has the right word for “you”?
exercises.explanation: Tú (you) has a mark; tu without it means “your”.

exercises.prompt: How is the h in hola pronounced?
exercises.explanation: Spanish h is never pronounced. Hola sounds like “ola”.

exercises.prompt: Which spelling is correct?
exercises.explanation: Ñ is a letter in its own right, and it changes the word.

exercises.prompt: Which is written correctly?
exercises.explanation: Languages are not capitalised in Spanish, though the first word of a sentence is.

lessons.title: 4. Numbers 0 to 30
lessons.subtitle: cero, uno, dos… treinta

explanations.title: Zero to fifteen
explanations.body: Learn these as separate words; there is no pattern to guess yet. Tap a row to hear it.

explanations.title: Sixteen to thirty
explanations.body: From 16 to 19 the number is built as ten + units and written as one word: dieciséis, diecisiete, dieciocho, diecinueve. Twenty is veinte, and 21 to 29 are one word too: veinte + units becomes veinti-. The accents on dieciséis, veintidós, veintitrés and veintiséis come from the stress rule.

explanations.title: Uno, un, una
explanations.body: Uno is the form used for counting. In front of a noun, uno shortens to un before a masculine noun and becomes una before a feminine one. The same happens inside 21, 31, 41…: veintiún libros, veintiuna sillas.

examples.text: Uno, dos, tres.
examples.translation: One, two, three.

examples.text: Hay un libro y una pluma.
examples.translation: There is a book and a pen.

examples.text: Hay veintiún alumnos.
examples.translation: There are twenty-one students.

examples.text: Hay veintiuna sillas.
examples.translation: There are twenty-one chairs.

exercises.prompt: Which word is 7?
exercises.explanation: Siete is 7. Seis is 6 and ocho is 8.

exercises.prompt: Which number is “quince”?
exercises.explanation: Quince is 15. Catorce is 14 and cinco is 5.

exercises.prompt: How do you write 12?
exercises.explanation: Doce is 12; once is 11 and trece is 13.

exercises.prompt: How do you write 18?
How do you write 22?
exercises.explanation: Veinte + dos fuses into one word, with an accent: veintidós.

exercises.prompt: What is dos más tres?
What is diez menos cuatro?
Hay ___ libro en la mesa.
exercises.explanation: Libro is masculine, so uno shortens to un.
exercises.promptTranslation: There is one book on the table.

exercises.prompt: Hay veintiún ___ en la clase.
exercises.explanation: Veintiún goes before a masculine noun, and the noun must be plural: alumnos. (Before feminine nouns, veintiuna is the usual form.)
exercises.promptTranslation: There are twenty-one students in the class.

exercises.prompt: Hay veintiuna ___ en el aula.
exercises.explanation: Veintiuna is feminine, so it needs a feminine plural noun: sillas.
exercises.promptTranslation: There are twenty-one chairs in the classroom.

lessons.title: 5. Numbers 31 to 100
lessons.subtitle: treinta y uno… noventa y nueve, cien

explanations.title: The tens
explanations.body: From 30 on, each ten has its own word. Cuarenta, cincuenta, sesenta, setenta, ochenta and noventa are all built on the number, with -nta. Tap a row to hear it.

explanations.title: Tens and units
explanations.body: Above 30 the pattern changes: it is written as three words, with y (“and”) in the middle. Twenty-one is one word (veintiuno), but thirty-one is treinta y uno. Cien (100) stands alone: it is the number used for counting and before a noun.

examples.text: treinta y uno
cuarenta y cinco
sesenta y ocho
noventa y nueve
Hay cien alumnos.
examples.translation: There are a hundred students.

examples.text: Tengo treinta y un años.
examples.translation: I am thirty-one years old.

explanations.title: Telephone numbers
explanations.body: Phone numbers are usually read one or two digits at a time, not as one big number. The groups differ from country to country, so listen for the pauses.

examples.text: cinco, veintiuno, cuarenta y tres
seis, trece, quince, diez

exercises.prompt: Which number is “cuarenta”?
How do you write 31?
exercises.explanation: Above 30: tens + y + units. (Before a noun uno becomes un: treinta y un libros.)

exercises.prompt: How do you write 45?
Which number is “setenta y seis”?
Which number is “ochenta”?
What is cincuenta más cincuenta?
Hay ___ alumnos en la escuela.
exercises.explanation: In front of a noun, 100 is cien.
exercises.promptTranslation: There are a hundred students at the school.

exercises.prompt: Mi abuelo tiene sesenta y ___ años.
exercises.explanation: Años is masculine plural, so uno shortens to un: sesenta y un años.
exercises.promptTranslation: My grandfather is sixty-one years old.

exercises.prompt: Which is the correct way to read the phone number 8-45-63?
options: ochenta y cuatro, cinco, sesenta y tres
ocho, cuarenta y cinco, sesenta y tres
exercises.explanation: Numbers are read in short groups, so each group is read as an ordinary number.

lessons.title: 6. The Spanish-speaking world
lessons.subtitle: Countries and capitals

explanations.title: Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean
explanations.body: Spanish is an official language in 20 countries, plus Puerto Rico. Learn each country with its capital. Many speakers also use an article with some country names (el Perú, la Argentina) but it is optional today, and you can leave it out.

tables.title: Norteamérica, Centroamérica y el Caribe
tables.note: Puerto Rico is a territory of the United States where Spanish is widely spoken.

explanations.title: South America, Europe and Africa
explanations.body: Bolivia has two capitals: Sucre is the constitutional one and La Paz is where the government sits, so La Paz is the answer most people give. Equatorial Guinea, in Central Africa, is the only Spanish-speaking country in Africa.

exercises.prompt: What is the capital of Chile?
exercises.explanation: Santiago is the capital of Chile. Lima is Peru’s, Quito Ecuador’s and Bogotá Colombia’s.

exercises.prompt: What is the capital of Cuba?
exercises.explanation: La Habana (Havana) is the capital of Cuba.

exercises.prompt: Which city is the capital of Argentina?
exercises.explanation: Montevideo is Uruguay’s and Asunción is Paraguay’s.

exercises.prompt: Which country has Madrid as its capital?
exercises.explanation: Madrid is in Spain, the only Spanish-speaking country in Europe.

exercises.prompt: Which Spanish-speaking country is in Africa?
exercises.explanation: Equatorial Guinea, whose capital is Malabo.

exercises.prompt: Which country is NOT in South America?
— ¿Cuál es la capital de Perú? — ___.
exercises.explanation: Lima is the capital of Peru.
exercises.promptTranslation: — What is the capital of Peru? — Lima.

exercises.prompt: La capital de Nicaragua es ___.
exercises.explanation: Managua, Nicaragua. Tegucigalpa is Honduras’s, San Salvador is El Salvador’s.
exercises.promptTranslation: The capital of Nicaragua is Managua.

exercises.prompt: Which is the capital of Puerto Rico?
exercises.explanation: San Juan. San José is in Costa Rica, Santo Domingo in the Dominican Republic.

lessons.title: 7. North, south, east, west
lessons.subtitle: al norte de, al sur de…

explanations.title: The compass
explanations.body: The four main directions are masculine: el norte, el sur, el este, el oeste. The in-between directions fuse the two: noroeste, noreste, suroeste, sureste. You will also see nordeste, sudeste and sudoeste. Map titles tend to use these.

explanations.title: X is north of Y
explanations.body: To place one thing in relation to another, use al + direction + de. Al is a + el: it means “to the”. You will study está (“is located”) in a later lesson; for now treat “X está al norte de Y” as a ready-made pattern. To ask where something is, say ¿Dónde está…?

examples.text: ¿Dónde está Bolivia?
examples.translation: Where is Bolivia?

examples.text: México está al norte de Guatemala.
examples.translation: Mexico is north of Guatemala.

examples.text: Chile está al oeste de Argentina.
examples.translation: Chile is west of Argentina.

examples.text: Uruguay está al este de Argentina.
examples.translation: Uruguay is east of Argentina.

examples.text: Ecuador está al sur de Colombia.
examples.translation: Ecuador is south of Colombia.

exercises.prompt: What does “el oeste” mean?
exercises.explanation: Oeste is west; este is east.

exercises.prompt: What does “el sureste” mean?
México está al ___ de Guatemala.
exercises.promptTranslation: Mexico is north of Guatemala.

exercises.prompt: Chile está al ___ de Argentina.
exercises.explanation: Chile is on the Pacific side of the Andes, west of Argentina.
exercises.promptTranslation: Chile is west of Argentina.

exercises.prompt: Uruguay está al ___ de Argentina.
exercises.explanation: Uruguay is across the Río de la Plata, east of Argentina.
exercises.promptTranslation: Uruguay is east of Argentina.

exercises.prompt: Colombia está al ___ de Ecuador.
exercises.promptTranslation: Colombia is north of Ecuador.

exercises.prompt: Costa Rica está al ___ de Nicaragua.
exercises.explanation: Costa Rica lies south of Nicaragua.
exercises.promptTranslation: Costa Rica is south of Nicaragua.

exercises.prompt: How do you ask where Peru is?
What does “al sur de” mean?
exercises.explanation: Al sur de Y = to the south of Y.

lessons.title: 8. In the classroom
lessons.subtitle: el libro, la mesa, el reloj…

explanations.title: Learn the article with the noun
explanations.body: Every Spanish noun is masculine or feminine, and the article shows which: el for masculine, la for feminine. Because the gender of an object is mostly arbitrary, learn each noun together with its article from the beginning: not “libro” but el libro.

explanations.title: On the desk and in the bag
explanations.body: Useful classroom nouns. Notice that audífonos (earphones) is almost always plural.

explanations.title: Same thing, different word
explanations.body: Spanish varies from country to country. Spain says el ordenador for the computer and el bolígrafo for the pen; Latin America mostly says la computadora, and Mexico says la pluma. The board is la pizarra in many places and el pizarrón in Mexico. Both are right, so use the word your teacher or the people around you use.

examples.text: la computadora
examples.translation: computer (Latin America)

examples.text: el ordenador
examples.translation: computer (Spain)

examples.text: el pizarrón
examples.translation: board (Mexico and elsewhere)

exercises.prompt: What does “la pared” mean?
What does “el techo” mean?
exercises.explanation: El techo is the ceiling or roof.

exercises.prompt: Which one do you use to write on the board?
exercises.explanation: A marker. El borrador is the eraser you use to clear the board.

exercises.prompt: Which one do you use to clear the board?
___ reloj está en la pared.
exercises.promptTranslation: The clock is on the wall.

exercises.prompt: ___ mochila está en la silla.
exercises.promptTranslation: The backpack is on the chair.

exercises.prompt: Hay ___ mapa en la clase.
exercises.explanation: Mapa is masculine (an exception to the -a rule), so un.
exercises.promptTranslation: There is a map in the class.

exercises.prompt: Which word is almost always plural?
exercises.explanation: Earphones come in a pair, so Spanish uses the plural.

exercises.prompt: In Spain, a computer is usually called…
exercises.explanation: Spain uses ordenador; Latin America says computadora.

lessons.title: 9. Classroom expressions
lessons.subtitle: Escuchen, lean, repita, por favor

explanations.title: What the teacher says
explanations.body: A teacher speaking to the whole class uses a command ending in -en (or -an): escuchen, lean, escriban, contesten. To one person, who is addressed as usted, the same verb loses its n: escuche, lea, escriba, conteste. Add por favor to be polite.

examples.text: ¿Comprenden?
examples.translation: Do you understand? (to the class)

examples.text: ¿Hay preguntas?
examples.translation: Are there any questions?

examples.text: Pase a la pizarra.
examples.translation: Come up to the board. (to one student)

explanations.title: What you say
explanations.body: These are the most useful sentences you can have ready in a Spanish class. Saying them in Spanish, rather than switching to English, is how you start thinking in the language.

rows: How do you say… in Spanish?

examples.text: ¿Qué quiere decir pared?
examples.translation: What does pared mean?

examples.text: ¿Cómo se escribe su nombre?
examples.translation: How do you spell your name?

exercises.prompt: You did not hear what the teacher said. What do you say?
exercises.explanation: Repita, por favor asks for a repetition. Tengo una pregunta announces a question.

exercises.prompt: The teacher says “Abran el libro.” What do you do?
exercises.explanation: Abrir = to open; cerrar = to close.

exercises.prompt: The teacher says “Cierren el libro.” What do you do?
Which sentence do you use if you want to ask the meaning of a word?
exercises.explanation: Qué quiere decir… = what does… mean? Cómo se escribe is for spelling.

exercises.prompt: The teacher asks you a question and you do not know the answer. You say…
exercises.explanation: No sé = I don’t know. No comprendo = I don’t understand.

exercises.prompt: Who is addressed in “Escriban”?
exercises.explanation: -an/-en endings address several people; -a/-e addresses one person, using usted.

exercises.prompt: ¿Cómo se ___ su nombre?
exercises.promptTranslation: How do you spell your name?

exercises.prompt: ¿Cómo se ___ ventana en inglés?
exercises.explanation: ¿Cómo se dice…? asks how to say something.
exercises.promptTranslation: How do you say ventana in English?

exercises.prompt: Which is said to ONE student?
exercises.explanation: Pase has no n, so it is addressed to one person.

lessons.title: 10. The: el, la, los, las
lessons.subtitle: Definite articles

explanations.title: Four words for “the”
explanations.body: English has one word for “the”. Spanish has four, because the article agrees with the noun in gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural).

examples.text: el alumno · la alumna
examples.translation: the male student · the female student

examples.text: los alumnos · las alumnas
examples.translation: the students (male or mixed) · the female students

explanations.title: Where Spanish says “the” and English does not
explanations.body: When you talk about something in a general sense, Spanish uses the article: it says “the music is important”, “the cats are small”. English leaves it out.

examples.text: La música es importante.
examples.translation: Music is important.

examples.text: Los gatos son pequeños.
examples.translation: Cats are small.

examples.text: El café es amargo.
examples.translation: Coffee is bitter.

explanations.title: Titles: about someone, or to someone
explanations.body: Before a title (señor, señora, doctor) + surname, use the article when you talk ABOUT the person. Leave it out when you speak TO the person.

exercises.prompt: Necesito ___ libros.
exercises.explanation: Libros is masculine plural, so los.
exercises.promptTranslation: I need the books.

exercises.prompt: ___ clase es interesante.
exercises.explanation: Clase is feminine singular, so la.
exercises.promptTranslation: The class is interesting.

exercises.prompt: ___ alumnos están en el aula.
exercises.explanation: Alumnos is masculine plural, so los.
exercises.promptTranslation: The students are in the classroom.

exercises.prompt: Las ___ están en la pared.
exercises.explanation: Las is feminine plural; it needs a feminine plural noun.
exercises.promptTranslation: The windows are in the wall.

exercises.prompt: Which article goes with “lápiz”?
How do you say “Music is important” in general?
exercises.explanation: Spanish uses the article for general statements.

exercises.prompt: You are talking ABOUT Mr. Rivera to a friend. Which is right?
exercises.explanation: Talking about someone: article + title + surname.

exercises.prompt: You are speaking TO Mr. Rivera. Which is right?
exercises.explanation: Speaking directly to someone, drop the article.

lessons.title: 11. A, an, some: un, una, unos, unas
lessons.subtitle: Indefinite articles

explanations.title: Four more words
explanations.body: The indefinite article means “a, an” in the singular and “some” in the plural. It agrees with the noun just like the definite article does.

explanations.title: A pen, then the pen
explanations.body: Use un/una for something new or unknown, and el/la once it is known. Unos/unas also mean “about” before a number: unos veinte alumnos.

examples.text: Hay una pluma en la mesa.
examples.translation: There is a pen on the table.

examples.text: La pluma es azul.
examples.translation: The pen is blue.

examples.text: Tengo unos libros y unas plumas.
examples.translation: I have some books and some pens.

examples.text: Hay unos veinte alumnos.
examples.translation: There are about twenty students.

exercises.prompt: Tengo ___ cuaderno.
exercises.promptTranslation: I have a notebook.

exercises.prompt: Hay ___ ventana en el aula.
exercises.promptTranslation: There is a window in the classroom.

exercises.prompt: Hay ___ sillas en la sala.
exercises.promptTranslation: There are some chairs in the room.

exercises.prompt: Hay ___ libros en la mesa.
exercises.promptTranslation: There are some books on the table.

exercises.prompt: Which word means “some” before feminine plural nouns?
exercises.explanation: Unas goes with feminine plurals; unos with masculine.

exercises.prompt: Hay ___ lápiz en la mesa. ___ lápiz es amarillo. Which pair fits?
exercises.explanation: First mention: un lápiz. Once it is known: el lápiz.
exercises.promptTranslation: There is a pencil on the table. The pencil is yellow.

exercises.prompt: What does “unos veinte alumnos” mean?
Which sentence is a first mention (new information)?
options: La mochila está en la silla.
Hay una mochila en la silla.
exercises.explanation: Hay + un/una introduces something new; the others talk about things already known.

lessons.title: 12. Nouns for people
lessons.subtitle: alumno, alumna, el estudiante, la estudiante

explanations.title: Masculine and feminine pairs
explanations.body: Spanish nouns are masculine or feminine. For people, the gender follows the person: men are masculine and women feminine. Most pairs differ only by the last letter: -o for men and -a for women. Words that end in a consonant in the masculine add -a for the feminine.

explanations.title: Same word for both
explanations.body: Nouns ending in -nte or -ista do not change. Only the article shows who is meant. One noun, persona, is always feminine, even when it means a man.

examples.text: Pedro es una persona simpática.
examples.translation: Pedro is a nice person.

exercises.prompt: What is the feminine of “el maestro”?
What is the feminine of “el profesor”?
exercises.explanation: The masculine ends in a consonant, so add -a.

exercises.prompt: What is the feminine of “el estudiante”?
exercises.explanation: Nouns in -nte keep the same form; only the article changes.

exercises.prompt: Which noun does NOT change between masculine and feminine?
exercises.explanation: -ista nouns are the same for both; only the article shows gender.

exercises.prompt: Marta es ___ buena amiga.
exercises.promptTranslation: Marta is a good friend.

exercises.prompt: Roberto es ___ estudiante nuevo.
exercises.explanation: Roberto is a man, so un estudiante.
exercises.promptTranslation: Roberto is a new student.

exercises.prompt: Carmen es ___ estudiante nueva.
exercises.explanation: Carmen is a woman, so una estudiante.
exercises.promptTranslation: Carmen is a new student.

exercises.prompt: Pedro is a man. Which sentence is correct?
exercises.explanation: Persona is always feminine, whoever it describes.

lessons.title: 13. Nouns for things: masculine or feminine?
lessons.subtitle: Endings, patterns and exceptions

explanations.title: Endings that point to the gender
explanations.body: For things there is no logic to gender, but the ending is a very good guide. Most nouns ending in -a, -ad, -ud and -ión are feminine. Most ending in -o, -l and -r are masculine. Tap a row to hear examples.

rows: la ventana · la mesa · la pluma
la ciudad · la dificultad · la salud
la lección · la canción · la opinión
el libro · el piso · el techo
el televisor · el calor · el color

explanations.title: Exceptions you will meet at once
explanations.body: Words of Greek origin ending in -ma are masculine: el problema, el tema, el idioma, el programa, el clima. Two of the most common nouns break the -a rule: el mapa and el día. And la mano is feminine although it ends in -o.

explanations.title: El aula, and words that change meaning
explanations.body:
Feminine nouns that begin with a stressed a- sound take el in the singular, to avoid two a’s clashing: el aula (the classroom), el agua (the water). They are still feminine: el agua fría (cold water), las aulas, las aguas.

A few nouns change meaning with the article: el capital is money, la capital is a city.

examples.text: El aula es grande.
examples.translation: The classroom is big.

examples.text: Madrid es la capital de España.
examples.translation: Madrid is the capital of Spain.

exercises.prompt: ___ ciudad es grande.
exercises.explanation: Ciudad ends in -ad, so it is feminine: la ciudad.
exercises.promptTranslation: The city is big.

exercises.prompt: ___ papel está en la mesa.
exercises.explanation: Papel ends in -l: masculine, el papel.
exercises.promptTranslation: The paper is on the table.

exercises.prompt: ___ lección es fácil.
exercises.promptTranslation: The lesson is easy.

exercises.prompt: ___ problema es grande.
exercises.explanation: Problema comes from Greek -ma and is masculine.
exercises.promptTranslation: The problem is big.

exercises.prompt: ___ día es largo.
exercises.explanation: Día is a famous exception: masculine despite -a.
exercises.promptTranslation: The day is long.

exercises.prompt: ___ aula es pequeña.
exercises.explanation: Aula is feminine (see pequeña), but before a stressed a- it takes el: el aula.
exercises.promptTranslation: The classroom is small.

exercises.prompt: Which noun is feminine although it ends in -o?
exercises.explanation: La mano. El mapa is masculine despite -a; libro and piso are regular -o nouns.

exercises.prompt: Which noun takes el?
exercises.explanation: Tema is Greek -ma: el tema. The others end in -ión/-ad and are feminine.

exercises.prompt: Which noun takes la?
exercises.explanation: -ud is a feminine ending: la salud. The others end in -r or -l.

exercises.prompt: What is “la capital de México”?
exercises.explanation: La capital is a city; el capital would be money.

lessons.title: 14. More than one: plural nouns
lessons.subtitle: -s, -es, and z → c

explanations.title: Three rules
explanations.body: To make a noun plural, look at its last letter. After a vowel, add -s. After a consonant, add -es. If it ends in -z, change the z to c and add -es. The article becomes plural too.

explanations.title: Accent marks move
explanations.body: Adding a syllable can change where the stress falls, so the written accent may disappear or appear. Words ending in -ión lose it: canción → canciones. A few gain one: joven → jóvenes. And país keeps its mark: países. Nouns that end in an unstressed -s do not change at all: el lunes, los lunes.

explanations.title: Mixed groups
explanations.body: When a group has both men and women, Spanish uses the masculine plural. Los profesores can be all men or a mixed group. Only los profesores y las profesoras names them separately.

examples.text: Los alumnos están en la clase.
examples.translation: The students (boys, or boys and girls) are in class.

examples.text: Las alumnas están en la clase.
examples.translation: The female students are in class.

exercises.prompt: Plural of “la pluma”?
Plural of “el capitán”?
exercises.explanation: Consonant ending: add -es. The accent is no longer needed.

exercises.prompt: Plural of “el lápiz”?
Plural of “la luz”?
Plural of “el reloj”?
Plural of “el papel”?
Plural of “la canción”?
exercises.explanation: -ión nouns lose the written accent in the plural.

exercises.prompt: Plural of “el país”?
exercises.explanation: País is stressed on the last syllable, and the plural países is stressed on í, so it keeps its mark.

exercises.prompt: What is the plural of “el lunes”?
exercises.explanation: Nouns ending in an unstressed -s do not change; only the article shows number.

exercises.prompt: A group of two men and one woman. Which is right?
exercises.explanation: Mixed groups use the masculine plural.

lessons.title: 15. I, you, he, she: subject pronouns
lessons.subtitle: yo, tú, usted, él, ella, nosotros, ustedes, ellos

explanations.title: The pronouns
explanations.body: A subject pronoun stands for the person doing the action. Spanish has more of them than English, mostly because it distinguishes “we” and “they” by gender and has two kinds of “you”.

tables.note: Usted is often written Ud., ustedes Uds. There is no pronoun for “it”: Spanish just uses the verb.

explanations.title: Tú or usted?
explanations.body:
Use tú (the “tuteo”) with friends, family, classmates and children. Use usted to show respect: to older people, superiors and strangers. If you are not sure, usted is the safe choice; a person who prefers tú will tell you, often by saying “tutéame”.

Customs vary: in some families and countries children use usted with their parents, and some couples address each other with usted. In Argentina, Uruguay and parts of Central America, vos replaces tú (el voseo). You will hear it, but you can use tú everywhere.

examples.text: ¿Cómo está usted, profesora?
examples.translation: How are you, professor? (formal)

examples.text: ¿Cómo estás tú, Pablo?
examples.translation: How are you, Pablo? (informal)

explanations.title: Plural “you”, and dropping the pronoun
explanations.body: In Latin America, ustedes is the only plural “you”, formal or familiar. In Spain, vosotros (vosotras for women) is used for friends and ustedes for formal address. Because the verb ending already shows the subject, Spanish normally leaves the pronoun out; use it only to clarify or to emphasise.

examples.text: Soy estudiante.
examples.translation: I am a student. (no pronoun needed)

examples.text: Yo soy estudiante; ella es profesora.
examples.translation: I am a student; she is a professor.

exercises.prompt: You talk to your teacher. Which “you” do you use?
exercises.explanation: A teacher is someone you address with respect: usted.

exercises.prompt: You talk to your best friend. Which “you” fits?
exercises.explanation: A friend gets the familiar tú.

exercises.prompt: You talk about yourself. Which pronoun?
You talk about your father. Which pronoun?
You talk about your mother. Which pronoun?
You and your friends talk about yourselves. Which pronoun?
exercises.explanation: Nosotros (nosotras for an all-female group) = we.

exercises.prompt: You talk about two girls. Which pronoun?
You talk about a mixed group of boys and girls. Which pronoun?
exercises.explanation: Mixed groups use the masculine form.

exercises.prompt: You speak to a group of friends in Madrid. Which pronoun is usual there?
exercises.explanation: In Spain vosotros is the familiar plural. (In Latin America you would use ustedes.)

exercises.prompt: Why does “Soy estudiante” need no yo?
options: The verb ending already shows the subject.
exercises.explanation: Soy can only mean “I am”, so yo is added only for emphasis.

lessons.title: 16. Verbs, and the verb ser
lessons.subtitle: soy, eres, es, somos, sois, son

explanations.title: Infinitives and endings
explanations.body:
A verb in its dictionary form is an infinitive. Spanish infinitives end in -ar, -er or -ir: trabajar, comer, vivir. To use a verb with a subject you conjugate it: the ending changes with the person and the tense (present, past, future).

Spanish has two verbs for “to be”: ser and estar. They are not interchangeable, and each has its own uses. Start with ser.

examples.text: trabajar
examples.translation: to work

examples.text: comer
examples.translation: to eat

examples.text: vivir
examples.translation: to live

explanations.title: Ser in the present
explanations.body: Ser is irregular: the forms do not follow a pattern, so learn them as they are. The third-person form es is shared by él, ella and usted; son is shared by ellos, ellas and ustedes.

examples.text: Tú eres mi amigo.
examples.translation: You are my friend.

examples.text: Nosotros somos amigos.
examples.translation: We are friends.

exercises.prompt: Yo ___ estudiante.
exercises.promptTranslation: I am a student.

exercises.prompt: Tú ___ mi amigo.
exercises.promptTranslation: You are my friend.

exercises.prompt: Ella ___ profesora.
exercises.explanation: Él, ella and usted take es.
exercises.promptTranslation: She is a professor.

exercises.prompt: Nosotros ___ amigos.
exercises.promptTranslation: We are friends.

exercises.prompt: Ustedes ___ de México.
exercises.explanation: Ustedes takes the same form as ellos: son.
exercises.promptTranslation: You (plural) are from Mexico.

exercises.prompt: Ellas ___ alumnas.
exercises.promptTranslation: They are students.

exercises.prompt: Usted ___ el profesor.
exercises.promptTranslation: You are the professor.

exercises.prompt: En España, vosotros ___ amigos.
exercises.promptTranslation: In Spain, you are friends.

exercises.prompt: Which pronoun does NOT go with “es”?
What does “eres” mean?
What is the infinitive ending of “comer”?

lessons.title: 17. Using ser: who, what, where from
lessons.subtitle: Identity, origin, nationality, occupation

explanations.title: Four jobs for ser
explanations.body: Ser says what someone or something is. In this chapter it has four main jobs. Ser de + a place gives origin, not where you are now.

explanations.title: Occupations take no article
explanations.body: After ser, a profession or other classification is used without un/una: Soy profesor, Mi hermana es médica. Add the article only when the noun is modified: Es un profesor excelente.

examples.text: Soy estudiante.
examples.translation: I am a student.

examples.text: Ana es ingeniera.
examples.translation: Ana is an engineer.

examples.text: Es un profesor excelente.
examples.translation: He is an excellent professor.

explanations.title: Questions that ser answers
explanations.body: These questions all take ser. Notice that the question word comes first and, in ¿De dónde…?, the preposition comes with it.

exercises.prompt: Ana ___ de Colombia.
exercises.explanation: Origin: ser de + place. Ana is third person: es.
exercises.promptTranslation: Ana is from Colombia.

exercises.prompt: Nosotros ___ de Perú.
exercises.promptTranslation: We are from Peru.

exercises.prompt: Mi amiga ___ ingeniera.
exercises.explanation: Occupation: ser. Mi amiga is third person: es.
exercises.promptTranslation: My friend is an engineer.

exercises.prompt: Tú ___ de Cuba, ¿verdad?
exercises.promptTranslation: You’re from Cuba, right?

exercises.prompt: Which is the usual way to say “I am a student”?
exercises.explanation: Professions and similar classifications are used without the article after ser.

exercises.prompt: How do you say “I’m from Chile”?
Which question asks where someone is from?
exercises.explanation: De dónde = from where. ¿Quién es usted? asks for identity.

exercises.prompt: When does a profession take un/una after ser?
exercises.explanation: Es un profesor excelente: the article comes back once the noun is described.

exercises.prompt: ¿Cuál es su nacionalidad? Which reply is correct?
exercises.explanation: Nationality is given with an adjective: peruano.

lessons.title: 18. Nationalities
lessons.subtitle: mexicano, mexicana, español, española…

explanations.title: A nationality is an adjective
explanations.body: In Spanish, nationalities are adjectives: they agree with the person (masculine or feminine, singular or plural) and are written with a small letter. Most end in -o for men and -a for women. Those that end in a consonant add -a for women (and lose any accent): español → española, francés → francesa, alemán → alemana.

explanations.title: More endings
explanations.body: Several Central American nationalities end in -eño/-eña or -eco/-eca. And a number end in -e or -ense: those stay the same for men and women.

examples.text: Mateo es colombiano y Sofía es colombiana.
examples.translation: Mateo is Colombian and Sofía is Colombian.

examples.text: Los señores son españoles.
examples.translation: The gentlemen are Spanish.

exercises.prompt: Carlos es de México. Es ___.
exercises.explanation: A man, so the masculine nationality adjective.
exercises.promptTranslation: Carlos is from Mexico. He is Mexican.

exercises.prompt: Ana es de Colombia. Es ___.
exercises.promptTranslation: Ana is from Colombia. She is Colombian.

exercises.prompt: Pierre es de Francia. Es ___.
exercises.promptTranslation: Pierre is from France. He is French.

exercises.prompt: Marta es de España. Es ___.
exercises.promptTranslation: Marta is from Spain. She is Spanish.

exercises.prompt: Hans es de Alemania. Es ___.
exercises.explanation: A man: alemán, with its accent.
exercises.promptTranslation: Hans is from Germany. He is German.

exercises.prompt: Laura y Rosa son de Costa Rica. Son ___.
exercises.promptTranslation: Laura and Rosa are from Costa Rica. They are Costa Rican.

exercises.prompt: Which nationality does NOT change for men and women?
exercises.explanation: -ense adjectives are the same for both genders.

exercises.prompt: What is the feminine of “inglés”?
What is the feminine of “hondureño”?
Which sentence is written correctly?

lessons.title: 19. The verb estar
lessons.subtitle: Location and how you are

explanations.title: Estar in the present
explanations.body: Estar is the second verb for “to be”. It is irregular only in the yo form (estoy) and in its written accents: estás, está, están. Because they end in a vowel, -n or -s, the stress rule would put the stress on the next-to-last syllable; they are stressed on the last one, so they carry a mark.

explanations.title: What estar is for
explanations.body: Estar tells you where something or someone is (location, with en) and how someone is (health and condition, with an adjective or adverb).

exercises.prompt: Yo ___ en la clase.
exercises.promptTranslation: I am in class.

exercises.prompt: Tú ___ en casa.
exercises.promptTranslation: You are at home.

exercises.prompt: La profesora ___ en el aula.
exercises.promptTranslation: The professor is in the classroom.

exercises.prompt: Nosotros ___ bien, gracias.
exercises.promptTranslation: We are fine, thanks.

exercises.prompt: Los libros ___ en la mochila.
exercises.promptTranslation: The books are in the backpack.

exercises.prompt: ¿Cómo ___ usted?
exercises.promptTranslation: How are you? (formal)

exercises.prompt: Which sentence tells where Chile is?
Which sentence asks how a friend is feeling?
exercises.explanation: Health and condition use estar. ¿Cómo eres? asks what you are like.

exercises.prompt: What does “estáis” mean?
exercises.explanation: Estáis is the vosotros form, used in Spain.

exercises.prompt: Why does “está” carry an accent?
options: It is stressed on the last syllable but ends in a vowel.
exercises.explanation: Words ending in a vowel are normally stressed on the next-to-last syllable, so a final stress is marked.

lessons.title: 20. Ser or estar?
lessons.subtitle: De for origin, en for location

explanations.title: Two verbs, two ideas
explanations.body: Both verbs translate as “to be”. A useful first rule: use ser to say what someone or something is (identity, origin, nationality, occupation) and estar to say where it is or how it is (location, health, condition). Their prepositions help too: ser goes with de for origin, estar goes with en for location.

explanations.title: Same city, different question
explanations.body: Compare ¿De dónde eres? (where do you come from) with ¿Dónde estás? (where are you right now). Soy de Chiapas says where you are from; Chiapas está en México says where Chiapas is. You can be from Madrid and be in Lima: soy de Madrid, estoy en Lima.

examples.text: Soy de Madrid, pero estoy en Lima.
examples.translation: I am from Madrid, but I’m in Lima.

examples.text: ¿De dónde eres?
examples.translation: Where are you from?

examples.text: ¿Dónde estás?
examples.translation: Where are you?

exercises.prompt: Mi amigo ___ de Colombia.
exercises.promptTranslation: My friend is from Colombia.

exercises.prompt: Bogotá ___ en Colombia.
exercises.promptTranslation: Bogotá is in Colombia.

exercises.prompt: Yo ___ estudiante.
exercises.promptTranslation: I am a student.

exercises.prompt: Nosotros ___ en la clase.
exercises.promptTranslation: We are in class.

exercises.prompt: ¿___ usted de México?
exercises.promptTranslation: Are you from Mexico?

exercises.prompt: ¿Cómo ___ tu madre hoy?
exercises.explanation: Asking how she is today: estar.
exercises.promptTranslation: How is your mother?

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
options: Los alumnos están en de Cuba.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
options: El profesor es de la oficina.
El profesor tiene en la oficina.
El profesor está en la oficina.
El profesor es en la oficina.

exercises.prompt: How do you ask where someone currently is?
Which preposition goes with ser to show origin?

lessons.title: 21. There is, there are: hay
lessons.subtitle: Hay un libro, no hay problema

explanations.title: Hay
explanations.body:
Hay means “there is” and “there are”. It is a special form of haber that never changes, whether what exists is singular or plural. It comes before the thing that exists: Hay un libro; Hay tres libros.

To make it negative, put no in front: No hay libros. To ask “how many are there?”, use ¿Cuántos…hay?

examples.text: Hay un profesor en la oficina.
examples.translation: There is a teacher in the office.

examples.text: Hay diez alumnos en la clase.
examples.translation: There are ten students in the class.

examples.text: No hay libros en la mesa.
examples.translation: There are no books on the table.

examples.text: ¿Cuántas sillas hay en el aula?
examples.translation: How many chairs are there in the classroom?

explanations.title: Hay or está?
explanations.body: Hay introduces something new, usually with un/una/unos/unas, a number or no article at all. Estar places something that is already known, usually with el, la, los, las, mi, tu or a name.

rows: Hay un reloj en la pared.
El reloj está en la pared.
Hay dos mochilas en la silla.
Las mochilas están en la silla.

exercises.prompt: ___ cinco alumnos en el aula.
exercises.explanation: There are five…: hay, which never changes.
exercises.promptTranslation: There are five students in the classroom.

exercises.prompt: ___ un mapa en la pared.
exercises.explanation: A new thing introduced with un: hay.
exercises.promptTranslation: There is a map on the wall.

exercises.prompt: El mapa ___ en la pared.
exercises.promptTranslation: The map is on the wall.

exercises.prompt: No ___ problema.
exercises.explanation: No hay problema = there is no problem.
exercises.promptTranslation: There is no problem.

exercises.prompt: ¿Cuántos libros ___ en la mochila?
exercises.promptTranslation: How many books are there in the backpack?

exercises.prompt: Does “hay” change for plural nouns?
options: No, hay is the same for singular and plural.
exercises.explanation: Hay is invariable: hay una silla, hay cinco sillas.

exercises.prompt: How do you say “There are no windows”?
exercises.explanation: No goes in front of hay.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence introduces something new?
options: Mi pluma está en la mesa.
Hay una pluma en la mesa.
La pluma está en la mesa.
Las plumas están en la mesa.
exercises.explanation: Hay + un/una introduces something that was not known.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence talks about something already known?
options: No hay llaves en la mesa.
Las llaves están en la mesa.
Hay unas llaves en la mesa.
exercises.explanation: A definite noun (las llaves) is placed with estar.

lessons.title: 22. The verb tener
lessons.subtitle: tengo, tienes, tiene, tenemos, tienen

explanations.title: Tener means to have
explanations.body: Tener expresses possession: Tengo tres libros. It is irregular in two ways: the yo form is tengo, and in the singular and in the third-person plural the e of the stem becomes ie (tienes, tiene, tienen). The nosotros and vosotros forms are regular: tenemos, tenéis.

examples.text: Tengo tres libros.
examples.translation: I have three books.

examples.text: ¿Tienes un teléfono?
examples.translation: Do you have a phone?

examples.text: Mi amiga tiene una computadora.
examples.translation: My friend has a computer.

exercises.prompt: Yo ___ dos amigos.
exercises.promptTranslation: I have two friends.

exercises.prompt: Tú ___ un lápiz.
exercises.promptTranslation: You have a pencil.

exercises.prompt: Ella ___ una pluma.
exercises.promptTranslation: She has a pen.

exercises.prompt: Nosotros ___ tres lápices.
exercises.promptTranslation: We have three pencils.

exercises.prompt: Los alumnos ___ libros.
exercises.promptTranslation: The students have books.

exercises.prompt: ¿Cuántos hermanos ___ usted?
exercises.promptTranslation: How many brothers and sisters do you have?

exercises.prompt: What does “tienen” mean?
In which forms does the e of tener change to ie?
exercises.explanation: Tienes, tiene, tienen change; tenemos and tenéis do not, and tengo is its own irregular form.

exercises.prompt: How do you ask a friend if they have a phone?
exercises.explanation: Tienes goes with tú. (¿Tiene un teléfono? would address usted.)

lessons.title: 23. Statements, negatives and yes/no questions
lessons.subtitle: No tengo, ¿tiene José un lápiz?

explanations.title: Word order and no
explanations.body: The usual order is subject – verb – object. To make a sentence negative, put no directly in front of the verb. Spanish has no word like English “do” or “does”: Do you have a pencil? is simply ¿Tienes un lápiz? with a question’s intonation.

explanations.title: Yes/no questions
explanations.body: There are two ways to make a question without a question word. Keep the statement's word order and raise your voice, or put the verb before the subject. Write both with ¿ and ?. If the answer is no, say no twice: once for the answer and once for the verb.

examples.text: ¿José tiene un lápiz?
examples.translation: Does José have a pencil?

examples.text: ¿Tiene José un lápiz?
examples.translation: Does José have a pencil? (verb first)

examples.text: No, José no tiene un lápiz.
examples.translation: No, José doesn’t have a pencil.

examples.text: Sí, José tiene un lápiz.
examples.translation: Yes, José has a pencil.

exercises.prompt: Where does “no” go in a negative sentence?
exercises.explanation: Yo no hablo: no sits right before the conjugated verb.

exercises.prompt: Which is correct?
Ella ___ tiene una pluma.
exercises.promptTranslation: She doesn’t have a pen.

exercises.prompt: ¿Tiene ___ un lápiz?
exercises.explanation: In a question the verb comes first, then the subject.
exercises.promptTranslation: Does José have a pencil?

exercises.prompt: Does Spanish use a helper verb like “do” in questions?
options: No. Intonation or word order makes the question.

exercises.prompt: ¿Tiene José un lápiz? Which answer means “No, he doesn’t”?
exercises.explanation: The first no answers; the second no negates the verb.

exercises.prompt: Which one is a yes/no question?
exercises.explanation: It has no question word, so the answer is sí or no.

exercises.prompt: Which written question is correct?
— ¿Eres de Chile? — No, ___ soy de Chile.
exercises.explanation: A negative answer repeats no before the verb.
exercises.promptTranslation: — Are you from Chile? — No, I’m not from Chile.

lessons.title: 24. Asking questions
lessons.subtitle: cómo, dónde, quién, cuándo, por qué

explanations.title: The question words
explanations.body: Question words always carry a written accent, and the question starts with them (or with a preposition + them). The voice falls at the end of an information question, as in a statement.

explanations.title: Por qué and porque
explanations.body: Why is two words with an accent: ¿por qué? Because is one word without: porque. They are the question and the answer to each other.

examples.text: ¿Por qué estudias español?
examples.translation: Why are you studying Spanish?

examples.text: Porque necesito la clase.
examples.translation: Because I need the class.

exercises.prompt: ¿___ está Chile? — En Sudamérica.
exercises.promptTranslation: Where is Chile?

exercises.promptTranslation: Why are you studying Spanish? — Because I need the class.

lessons.title: 25. Asking questions, part 2
lessons.subtitle: qué or cuál, plurals, cuánto and friends

explanations.title: Qué or cuál?
explanations.body: Both can be “what”. Use qué when you want a definition or general information: ¿Qué es un diccionario? Use cuál when you choose from a range or ask for a personal fact, such as a name, address or phone number. Before a noun, qué is the standard choice: ¿Qué libro necesitas?

rows: a specific piece of personal information

explanations.title: Plurals and agreement
explanations.body: Quién, cuál and cuánto have forms for number: ¿Quiénes son tus amigos? ¿Cuáles son tus libros? Cuánto also agrees in gender, like an adjective: cuánto dinero, cuánta agua, cuántos libros, cuántas mesas.

explanations.title: Prepositions go first
explanations.body: In English you can end a question with a preposition (“Where is she from?”). Spanish never does: the preposition moves to the front, right before the question word.

examples.text: ¿De dónde es Antonio?
examples.translation: Where is Antonio from?

examples.text: ¿Con quién hablas?
examples.translation: Who are you talking to?

examples.text: ¿En qué aula está Nico?
examples.translation: Which classroom is Nico in?

exercises.prompt: ¿___ es un diccionario?
exercises.promptTranslation: What is a dictionary?

exercises.prompt: ¿___ es tu número de teléfono?
exercises.promptTranslation: What is your phone number?

exercises.prompt: ¿___ son tus libros?
exercises.promptTranslation: Which ones are your books?

exercises.prompt: ¿___ son tus amigos?
exercises.promptTranslation: Who are your friends?

exercises.prompt: ¿Cuántas ___ hay en el aula?
exercises.promptTranslation: How many tables are there in the classroom?

exercises.prompt: ¿Cuánto ___ tiene usted?
exercises.promptTranslation: How much money do you have?

exercises.prompt: ¿Cuántos ___ tienes?
exercises.promptTranslation: How many brothers and sisters do you have?

exercises.prompt: Which is the correct way to ask where Antonio is from?
exercises.explanation: Spanish never ends with the preposition; it goes in front of the question word.

exercises.prompt: Which is the correct way to ask who you speak with?
When do you use “cuáles”?
options: When the thing you ask about is plural.
exercises.explanation: Cuáles is the plural of cuál.

lessons.title: 26. Cognates and false friends
lessons.subtitle: importante, but also embarazada…

explanations.title: Words you already know
explanations.body: Cognates are words in two languages that look alike and mean the same, and Spanish and English share thousands. Many follow patterns: English -tion becomes -ción (nation → nación); -ty becomes -dad (university → universidad); -ous becomes -oso (famous → famoso); -ant and -ent become -ante and -ente (important → importante, excellent → excelente). Always check the gender too: la información, el hospital.

explanations.title: False friends
explanations.body: Some words look alike but mean something different. These are false cognates (falsos amigos), and a few of them can cause real trouble.

tables.note: “Embarrassed” is avergonzado or, informally, con vergüenza. Never say estoy embarazada for “I’m embarrassed”.

exercises.prompt: What does “éxito” mean?
exercises.explanation: Éxito = success. An exit is a salida.

exercises.prompt: What does “librería” mean?
What does “actual” mean?
What does “carpeta” mean?
What does “asistir a una clase” mean?
What does “constipado” mean?
exercises.explanation: Constipado is about a stuffy nose.

exercises.prompt: What does “ropa” mean?

exercises.explanation: Importante has the same meaning as English “important”.

exercises.prompt: Which English word becomes “-ción”?
A woman says “Estoy embarazada” when she is embarrassed. What does she actually say?
exercises.explanation: Embarazada means pregnant, so the sentence has a very different meaning.

lessons.title: 27. Review: personal information
lessons.subtitle: Greetings, ser, estar, tener, hay and questions

explanations.title: A formal introduction
explanations.body: Read this dialogue aloud and notice how the verbs and the formal address fit together: ¿cómo está usted?, ¿de dónde es usted?

explanations.body: The same ideas, with tú and a more casual tone.

lessons.title: 28. La familia
lessons.subtitle: madre, padre, hermanos, abuelos, tíos, primos

explanations.title: Close family
explanations.body: Most family words come in masculine and feminine pairs. The masculine plural covers both: los padres is “parents” (mother and father), los hermanos is “brothers and sisters”, los hijos is “children” (sons and daughters), los abuelos “grandparents”, los tíos “aunts and uncles”, los primos “cousins”.

tables.note: La mujer means both “woman” and “wife”; el hombre means “man”.

explanations.title: In-laws, step-family and more
explanations.body: Spanish uses -astro/-astra for step-relatives and the words below for in-laws. A godparent is padrino or madrina; a boyfriend or fiancé is novio, a girlfriend or fiancée is novia.

exercises.prompt: Rafael y Lucía tienen dos hijos, Inés y Tomás. What is Inés to Lucía?
Tomás es el ___ de Inés.
exercises.explanation: Tomás and Inés have the same parents.
exercises.promptTranslation: Tomás is Inés’s brother.

exercises.explanation: Your mother’s parents are your grandparents.

exercises.explanation: A parent’s sister is your aunt.

exercises.explanation: Your aunt’s child is your cousin.

exercises.promptTranslation: Hugo is Lucía’s nephew.

exercises.explanation: The masculine plural includes both genders.

What is the wife of your son?

lessons.title: 29. Whose is it? De and del
lessons.subtitle: la pluma de la profesora, el padre del director

explanations.title: No apostrophe-s
explanations.body: Spanish has no ’s. To show who owns something, or how people are related, put de between the two nouns. The order is reversed compared with English: the thing first, then the owner.

examples.text: la pluma de la profesora
examples.translation: the teacher’s pen

examples.text: la esposa de mi hermano
examples.translation: my brother’s wife

examples.text: los libros de Ana
examples.translation: Ana’s books

examples.text: ¿De quién es la mochila?
examples.translation: Whose backpack is it?

examples.text: Es de Pedro.
examples.translation: It’s Pedro’s.

explanations.title: De + el = del
explanations.body: When de meets the article el, the two words merge into del. De la, de los and de las do not contract. Be careful: de él (“his”, “of him”) stays separate, because there él is a pronoun with an accent.

examples.text: La esposa del profesor es ingeniera.
examples.translation: The professor’s wife is an engineer.

exercises.prompt: How do you say “the teacher’s pen” (a female teacher)?
la casa ___ mis padres
exercises.explanation: Mis is not el, so no contraction: de mis padres.

exercises.promptTranslation: the doctor’s daughter

exercises.prompt: How do you ask “Whose pen is it?”
How do you say “It’s Ana’s”?
Which is correct?

lessons.title: 30. My, your, his: possessive adjectives
lessons.subtitle: mi, tu, su, nuestro, vuestro

explanations.title: The possessives
explanations.body: Possessive adjectives come before the noun. Mi, tu and su change only for number: they agree with the thing owned (mis libros). Nuestro and vuestro also change for gender.

rows: your (usted, ustedes), his, her, its, their

examples.text: mi hijo · mis hijos
examples.translation: my son · my sons

examples.text: nuestra hija · nuestras hijas
examples.translation: our daughter · our daughters

explanations.title: The owner does not matter
explanations.body: The adjective agrees with what is owned, not with the owner. A woman says mi padre; two brothers say nuestra madre. Because su means his, her, your (formal) and their, you can clarify with de él, de ella, de usted, de ellos: la casa de ella.

examples.text: Mi padre es ingeniero.
examples.translation: My father is an engineer.

examples.text: Tus hermanas son simpáticas.

exercises.promptTranslation: I live with my family.

exercises.explanation: Padres is plural and tú: tus.

exercises.explanation: De ella states whose house it is.

exercises.prompt: Which is correct for “your (tú) books”?
exercises.explanation: Libros is plural; tu has no accent.

lessons.title: 31. Family events and marital status
lessons.subtitle: soltero, casado, la boda, el cumpleaños

explanations.title: Marital status
explanations.body: Soltero/a, casado/a, divorciado/a and viudo/a are adjectives, so they agree with the person. With marital status, speakers use both ser and estar: es casado suggests a settled status, está casado a state that can change. The difference is subtle, and many speakers use either.

examples.text: Mi hermano es casado.
examples.translation: My brother is married.

examples.text: Mi tía está divorciada.
examples.translation: My aunt is divorced.

explanations.title: Celebrations
explanations.body: These words name the big family events. To say when your birthday is, Spanish uses cumplir años (literally “to complete years”): Cumplo años en abril. Greet someone with ¡Feliz cumpleaños! or ¡Felicidades!

examples.text: La niña nace en un hospital.
examples.translation: The baby girl is born in a hospital.

examples.text: Cumplo años en abril.
examples.translation: My birthday is in April.

examples.text: ¡Feliz cumpleaños!
examples.translation: Happy birthday!

A man whose wife has died is…

exercises.promptTranslation: My mother and father are married.

lessons.title: 32. Regular -ar verbs in the present
lessons.subtitle: hablo, hablas, habla, hablamos, hablan

explanations.title: Stem + ending
explanations.body: To conjugate a regular -ar verb, drop -ar and add -o, -as, -a, -amos, -áis, -an to the stem. The stem never changes in regular verbs, so once you know the endings you can use hundreds of verbs. Spanish has one present tense for both “I speak” and “I am speaking”.

explanations.title: Common -ar verbs
explanations.body: Notice how much a single ending does: in estudio español, the -o already says “I”.

exercises.promptTranslation: I study Spanish.

exercises.promptTranslation: You talk with your mother.

lessons.title: 33. Regular -er and -ir verbs
lessons.subtitle: como, comes, come, comemos, comen · vivo, vives…

explanations.title: Two groups, almost one pattern
explanations.body: -er and -ir verbs share every ending except nosotros and vosotros. Drop -er or -ir and add -o, -es, -e, then -emos/-éis (for -er) or -imos/-ís (for -ir), and finally -en.

explanations.title: Common -er and -ir verbs
explanations.body: Verbs like leer, correr, beber, aprender, vender and escribir, abrir, recibir, compartir all use these endings.

lessons.title: 34. Regular verbs at work
lessons.subtitle: Questions, answers and everyday sentences

explanations.title: Question and answer: same verb, new subject
explanations.body: In a conversation the verb you hear in the question comes back in the answer, but with the ending that fits the new speaker. Question to tú or usted, answer in yo.

rows: Mi familia vive en Nueva York.
Mis padres trabajan en un hospital.
Sí, hablo con ellos los domingos.

explanations.title: When and how often
explanations.body: Time words say when or how often. They go at the start or end of the sentence, and siempre (always) and nunca (never) go right before the verb. A single nunca already makes the sentence negative, with no extra no.

lessons.title: 35. Adjectives: masculine and feminine
lessons.subtitle: alto, alta; trabajador, trabajadora; inteligente

explanations.title: An adjective agrees with its noun
explanations.body: An adjective describes a noun or pronoun and must match its gender and number: un profesor nuevo, una profesora nueva. How an adjective changes depends on its ending.

rows: a nationality ending in a consonant

explanations.title: Matching the noun
explanations.body: The adjective follows the noun (more on that next lesson) and agrees with it, not with the speaker. Adjectives that do not change for gender (inteligente, azul) still change for number.

examples.text: El profesor nuevo es alto.
examples.translation: The new teacher is tall.

examples.text: La profesora nueva es alta.
examples.translation: The new teacher is tall. (female)

examples.text: El marinero es inteligente.
examples.translation: The sailor is intelligent.

examples.text: La señora es trabajadora y tímida.

exercises.promptTranslation: The student is tall.

exercises.promptTranslation: The (female) student is tall.

exercises.explanation: Adjectives in -or add -a for the feminine.

lessons.title: 36. Adjectives: plural and position
lessons.subtitle: libros nuevos, una casa grande, un buen amigo

explanations.title: Plural adjectives
explanations.body: Plural adjectives are formed like plural nouns: add -s after a vowel, -es after a consonant, and change -z to -ces. For a mixed group, use the masculine plural.

examples.text: Mis padres son trabajadores y optimistas.
examples.translation: My parents are hard-working and optimistic.

explanations.title: Where adjectives go
explanations.body:
Most adjectives follow the noun: un hombre delgado, una silla marrón. A few change meaning if they come first, and some lose their ending before a masculine noun.

Bueno and malo become buen and mal before a masculine singular noun (un buen amigo). Grande becomes gran before any singular noun and then means “great” rather than “big”.

exercises.prompt: Los libros son ___.
exercises.promptTranslation: The books are new.

exercises.prompt: Las casas son ___.
exercises.promptTranslation: The houses are big.

exercises.prompt: Mis amigas son ___.
exercises.promptTranslation: My friends are nice.

exercises.prompt: Hay una pluma ___ en la mesa.
exercises.explanation: Adjective after the noun, feminine singular.
exercises.promptTranslation: There is a red pen on the table.

exercises.prompt: Tiene dos libros ___.
exercises.explanation: Libros is masculine plural, and the adjective follows it.
exercises.promptTranslation: He has two new books.

exercises.prompt: Es un ___ amigo.
exercises.explanation: Bueno shortens to buen before a masculine singular noun.
exercises.promptTranslation: He is a good friend.

exercises.prompt: Plural of “feliz”?
Plural of “popular”?
Which is the usual position for adjectives that describe?
options: at the end of the sentence
exercises.explanation: Descriptive adjectives normally follow the noun.

exercises.prompt: Which phrase means “a grand house”?
exercises.explanation: Gran before the noun carries the meaning “great”; after it, grande means “big”.

lessons.title: 37. Describing people: how they look
lessons.subtitle: alto, delgado, pelo castaño, ojos azules

explanations.title: Build and age
explanations.body: Use ser + adjective for height, build and age, and tener for features such as hair, eyes and a beard. Describing bodies can be blunt in any language: delgado, fuerte and de mediana estatura are neutral choices, and many people avoid gordo.

tables.note: De mediana estatura means medium height. Mayor means older; menor, younger.

explanations.title: Hair, eyes and skin
explanations.body: Hair, eyes and skin come with tener. Colours and shapes agree with the noun: el pelo castaño, los ojos azules, la piel morena.

rows: el pelo castaño · rubio · negro · canoso
los ojos azules · verdes · castaños · negros

examples.text: Mi hermana es alta y delgada.
examples.translation: My sister is tall and thin.

examples.text: Tiene el pelo largo y rizado.
examples.translation: She has long, curly hair.

lessons.title: 39. Colors
lessons.subtitle: rojo, azul, verde, amarillo…

explanations.title: The colors
explanations.body: Colors are adjectives. Those ending in -o change like any -o adjective (rojo, roja, rojos, rojas). Azul, verde, gris, café and marrón do not change for gender, and add -es in the plural if they end in a consonant. Because colors follow the noun, say una pluma roja, not “a red pen” word for word.

explanations.title: Light and dark; flags
explanations.body: Add claro (light) or oscuro (dark) after the color: azul claro, verde oscuro. These pairs stay unchanged for gender. A flag is la bandera, so its colors are feminine: blanca, roja.

lessons.title: 40. And and or: y/e, o/u
lessons.subtitle: Isabel y Fernando, Fernando e Isabel

explanations.title: Y becomes e; o becomes u
explanations.body: Y means “and” and o means “or”. To avoid two identical vowel sounds in a row, y changes to e before a word that begins with the sound i (i or hi), and o changes to u before a word that begins with the sound o (o or ho).

rows: hijos sounds like it begins with i
hombre sounds like it begins with o
tables.note: The exception is the sound “hie”: agua y hielo keeps y. And in a question beginning ¿Y…?, the y stays.

explanations.title: Spelling vs sound
explanations.body: The rule follows the sound, not the spelling. Hijos and Isabel begin with the vowel sound i (the h is silent), so e. Ocho begins with the vowel sound o, so u: siete u ocho.

lessons.title: 41. Numbers 100–1000
lessons.subtitle: cien, ciento diez, doscientos, quinientos

explanations.title: The hundreds
explanations.body: Cien is exactly one hundred. For 101 to 199 use ciento, then add the rest: ciento uno, ciento veinte, ciento noventa y nueve. The other hundreds are single words.

tables.note: Watch the irregular ones: quinientos (not cincocientos), setecientos (not sietecientos) and novecientos (not nuevecientos).

explanations.title: Rules for hundreds
explanations.body: From 200 to 900, the hundreds agree in gender with the noun that follows: doscientos libros, doscientas plumas. Cien is also the form you use when you count (noventa, cien) and before a noun: cien alumnos.

explanations.title: Writing numbers
explanations.body: Most Spanish-speaking countries use a period where English uses a comma, and a comma where English uses a decimal point. So 1.000 is one thousand, and 0,25 is read “cero coma veinticinco”.

tables.note: Never say “un mil” for 1.000. It is just mil.

lessons.title: 42. First, second, third: ordinals
lessons.subtitle: primero, segundo, tercero…

explanations.title: Ordinal numbers, 1 to 10
explanations.body: Ordinals say the order of things. They have masculine and feminine forms, just like adjectives: el cuarto piso, la cuarta clase.

explanations.title: Primer, tercer; and after ten
explanations.body:
Primero and tercero drop the final -o before a masculine singular noun, just like bueno and malo: el primer día, el tercer piso. The feminine keeps its ending: la primera vez.

Ordinals are rarely used past ten. Spanish uses the ordinary number after the noun: el piso quince, el siglo veinte.

lessons.title: 43. Days of the week
lessons.subtitle: lunes, martes, miércoles…

explanations.title: The seven days
explanations.body: Days of the week are not capitalized in Spanish. On most Spanish calendars the week begins on Monday. All the days are masculine. Lunes to viernes are the same in the singular and the plural; sábado and domingo just add -s.

tables.note: Saturday and Sunday together are el fin de semana (the weekend).

explanations.title: On Monday, on Mondays
explanations.body: English says “on”: on Monday, on Mondays. Spanish uses the article instead. Use el for one particular day and los for something that happens every week.

lessons.title: 44. Months, seasons and dates

explanations.title: The twelve months
explanations.body: Months are masculine and are not capitalized in Spanish.

tables.note: Use en for months and seasons: en mayo, en verano.

explanations.title: Saying the date
explanations.body:
The pattern is el + number + de + month. Use the ordinary number, except for the first of the month, where many speakers say primero. To ask the date, use ¿Qué fecha es hoy? or ¿Cuál es la fecha de hoy?

The numbers 21 to 29 are one word: veintiuno, veintidós, veintitrés. After thirty they are three words: treinta y uno.

explanations.title: Spanish “has” years
explanations.body: To give your age, Spanish uses tener, not ser. You literally have years: Tengo veinte años. To ask someone’s age, use ¿Cuántos años tienes? (informal) or ¿Cuántos años tiene? (formal).

lessons.title: 48. What do you do? Jobs

explanations.title: Jobs with a masculine and a feminine form
explanations.body: Most job titles follow the pattern you know from nouns for people: -o becomes -a, and a consonant adds -a.

explanations.title: One form for both
explanations.body: As with estudiante and periodista, a few job titles are the same for men and women. Only the article changes.

explanations.title: Asking and answering
explanations.body:
To ask what someone does for a living, use ¿A qué se dedica usted? (formal) or ¿A qué te dedicas? (informal). You can also ask ¿Qué hace tu padre? To answer, use ser plus the job, with no article: Mi padre es mecánico.

If you add an adjective or other description, the article comes back: Mi tío es un mecánico excelente.

lessons.title: 50. Numbers over 1000

explanations.title: Thousands
explanations.body: Mil is one thousand, and it never changes: dos mil, tres mil, diez mil. For a number like 1.150 you say mil, then the hundreds: mil ciento cincuenta.

explanations.title: Millions and a trap
explanations.body: Millón is a noun, so it has a plural: un millón, dos millones. When a noun follows, add de: un millón de personas. Mil millones is one billion in English; un billón is one trillion — billón is a false friend of English “billion”.

lessons.title: 51. What time is it?
lessons.subtitle: Son las tres y media

explanations.title: Es la una, son las dos
explanations.body: To ask the time, say ¿Qué hora es? The answer begins with Es la for one o’clock and with Son las for every other hour. After the hour, y adds minutes up to half past, and menos subtracts them after the half.

explanations.title: Noon, midnight and polite questions
explanations.body: Noon is mediodía and midnight is medianoche; both go with es. A polite way to ask is Disculpe, ¿qué hora tiene? Informally you can also say ¿Qué hora tienes?

explanations.title: A la una, a las dos
explanations.body: To say when something happens, use a. The pattern follows the clock: a la una for one o’clock, a las dos, a las tres for the rest. To ask, say ¿A qué hora…?

explanations.title: Morning, afternoon, night
explanations.body: After a specific time, use de la mañana, de la tarde or de la noche. When no time is mentioned, use por la or en la: trabajo por la mañana. For a span of time use de…a or desde…hasta.

explanations.title: Hacer is regular except for yo
explanations.body: Hacer means “to do” or “to make”. Only the yo form is irregular (hago); the rest follow the -er pattern, so they are easy.

explanations.title: Hacer in daily life
explanations.body: Hacer appears in many everyday phrases: hacer la tarea (do homework), hacer ejercicio (exercise), hacer una pregunta (ask a question), hacer la cama (make the bed). It is also the verb in ¿Qué hace usted?, which asks about someone’s job.

lessons.title: 55. This, that, that over there
lessons.subtitle: este, ese, aquel

explanations.title: Three distances
explanations.body: Spanish has three demonstrative adjectives, not two. Este means “this” (near me), ese means “that” (a bit farther, near you) and aquel means “that over there” (far from both of us). They agree with the noun in gender and number, and they come before it.

explanations.title: Choosing the right one
explanations.body: Pick the distance first, then match the noun. If the noun is feminine singular, use esta, esa or aquella; if it is masculine plural, use estos, esos or aquellos, and so on.

explanations.title: Demonstrative pronouns
explanations.body: If you drop the noun, the demonstrative stands alone as a pronoun and means “this one, that one”. The forms are exactly the same, and they still agree with the noun you left out. Older texts put an accent on the pronouns (éste); the modern rule no longer asks for it.

explanations.title: Hay que + infinitive
explanations.body: Hay que followed by an infinitive says that something must be done, without saying who must do it. It is impersonal: the form never changes, whatever the subject.

lessons.title: 58. Joining sentences with que

explanations.title: Que means that, which, who
explanations.body: The word que joins two ideas into one sentence. It stands for “that”, “which” or “who”. In English you can often leave it out, but in Spanish que is always required.

Vivo en una casa que es muy grande.

explanations.title: English can skip it, Spanish cannot
explanations.body: English often drops the word: “a school (that is) called Cervantes”. Spanish keeps que every time, so a school called Cervantes is una escuela que se llama Cervantes.

explanations.body: A and el are never written apart: they merge into al. This happens before any masculine singular noun (al banco, al profesor), except in names that include El, such as El Salvador. With la, los and las, nothing changes.

explanations.body: Adónde asks where to; De dónde asks where from. Use them with ir and ser.

explanations.title: Tener que + infinitive

explanations.body: Tener que is personal: it names who has to do it. Hay que is impersonal: it is a general rule for everyone.

explanations.title: More than, less than, as…as
explanations.body: To compare two things, put más (more) or menos (less) before the adjective and que (than) after it. For equality, use tan + adjective + como.

explanations.title: Everything must match
explanations.body: In Spanish an article, a noun and its adjective share gender and number. Possessives (mi, tu, su, nuestro) agree with the noun they describe, not with the owner. Mi and tu and su only change for number; nuestro changes for gender too.

explanations.title: Small things to remember
explanations.body: Adjectives ending in -e or a consonant (grande, azul) keep the same form for masculine and feminine and only add -s or -es in the plural. Before a word starting with the sound i, y becomes e: padres e hijos.

explanations.title: Three steps to the right form

explanations.title: The irregular ones so far
