explanations.title: More o → ue verbs
explanations.body: Almorzar (to have lunch), contar (to count, to tell), costar (to cost), encontrar (to find) and soñar (to dream) follow the same pattern. Jugar changes u to ue: juego, juegas, juega, jugamos, jugáis, juegan. In Spain, jugar takes a plus the sport (juego al fútbol); in much of Latin America people also say juego fútbol.

explanations.title: Querer has two meanings
explanations.body: Querer followed by an infinitive means “to want to”. Querer followed by a (the personal a) and a person means “to love, to care for”, in family and romantic love alike. Amar a is a deeper, more passionate love, often for a partner or for something very important.

explanations.title: Me encanta
explanations.body: Encantar says you love something in the sense of liking it a lot. It works like a fixed phrase: me encanta + one thing, me encantan + several things. You will meet the full pattern later, so for now use it just like this.

explanations.title: Feelings: Spanish has, English is
explanations.body: Many physical conditions and feelings use tener plus a noun, where English uses “to be” plus an adjective. You say tengo frío (literally “I have cold”), not estoy frío. Because the feeling is a noun, you describe how much with mucho or mucha, never with muy.

lessons.title: 93. Por and para, part 1

explanations.title: Two ways to say “for”
explanations.body: Por and para both translate as “for”, but they have different jobs. Start with four.

explanations.title: Quick test
explanations.body: Ask what the “for” really means. If it means “in exchange for” or “by means of”, use por. If it means “intended for” a person or “in order to” do something, use para. To say you travel in a vehicle, use en, not por: voy en autobús.

explanations.title: From adjective to adverb
explanations.body: Many adverbs end in -mente, which works like the English ending that makes adverbs. If the adjective ends in -o, use the feminine form (-a) and add -mente. If it ends in -e or a consonant, just add -mente. A written accent in the adjective stays in the adverb.

lessons.title: 98. Weather with hacer
lessons.subtitle: ¿Qué tiempo hace? Hace calor. Hace buen tiempo.

explanations.title: ¿Qué tiempo hace?
explanations.body: To ask about the weather, say ¿Qué tiempo hace? Many answers use hace (from hacer) plus a noun. Spanish has no word for “it” here: the verb is simply hace, always in the singular.

explanations.title: Mucho, not muy
explanations.body: Calor, frío, sol and viento are nouns here, so “very” is mucho (mucho calor), never muy. Bueno and malo drop their final -o before a masculine singular noun: buen tiempo, mal tiempo.

examples.text: Hoy hace mucho calor en la playa.
examples.translation: Today it is very hot at the beach.

examples.text: ¿Qué tiempo hace en Quito hoy?
examples.translation: What is the weather like in Quito today?

examples.text: Hace mucho viento y necesito una chaqueta.
examples.translation: It is very windy and I need a jacket.

examples.text: Vamos al parque porque hace buen tiempo.
examples.translation: We are going to the park because the weather is nice.

explanations.title: The weather, or how you feel
explanations.body: For the weather, use hacer: Hace frío. For how a person feels, use tener: Tengo frío means “I am cold”.

exercises.prompt: Hoy ___ mucho calor.
exercises.explanation: Weather with a noun uses hacer: hace calor.
exercises.promptTranslation: Today it is very hot.

exercises.prompt: En enero ___ mucho frío en Chicago.
exercises.explanation: The weather verb is always third person singular: hace.
exercises.promptTranslation: In January it is very cold in Chicago.

exercises.prompt: Vamos a la playa porque hace ___ tiempo.
exercises.explanation: Before a masculine noun, bueno becomes buen.
exercises.promptTranslation: We are going to the beach because the weather is nice.

exercises.prompt: No salimos porque hace ___ tiempo.
exercises.explanation: Before a masculine noun, malo becomes mal.
exercises.promptTranslation: We are not going out because the weather is bad.

exercises.prompt: How do you say “It is very windy”?
exercises.explanation: Viento is a noun here, so mucho (not muy), and the verb is hace.

exercises.explanation: ¿Qué tiempo hace? is the standard question.

Mi hermano ___ mucho frío y lleva un abrigo.

lessons.title: 99. Weather with estar and hay
lessons.subtitle: Está nublado. Hay tormenta. Hay niebla.

explanations.title: Estar + adjective: the sky
explanations.body: To describe how the sky looks, use estar with an adjective. Está nublado means the sky is cloudy; está despejado means it is clear, with no clouds.

explanations.title: Hay + noun: something is happening
explanations.body: Hay means “there is” or “there are”. Use it for weather events: it never changes, even when the noun is plural.

rows: There is snow in the mountains.

examples.text: Hoy hay mucha niebla en la carretera.
examples.translation: Today there is a lot of fog on the road.

examples.text: Hay tormentas en el mar.
examples.translation: There are storms at sea.

explanations.title: Which verb?
explanations.body: Use hacer for temperature, sun and wind. Use estar for the look of the sky. Use hay for events and things in the air. Learn each phrase whole, as one block. (Hay sol and hay viento are also common; hace is the safest choice.)

lessons.title: 100. Weather verbs: llueve, nieva, truena
lessons.subtitle: Llueve. Nieva. Truena. Llovizna.

explanations.title: Verbs with no subject
explanations.body: Some weather is expressed with a single verb that exists only in the third person singular. Llover and nevar are boot verbs: llueve and nieva.

explanations.title: In a sentence
explanations.body: These verbs take adverbs like mucho and poco. To say that it is happening right now, you can use estar + the -ndo form of the verb: Está lloviendo.

lessons.title: 101. Seasons and months
lessons.subtitle: la primavera, el verano, el otoño, el invierno

explanations.title: The four seasons
explanations.body: Seasons are estaciones. Learn the gender: la primavera, el verano, el otoño, el invierno. You can say en verano or en el verano; both are normal.

rows: Hay flores y a veces llueve.
Hace fresco y los árboles pierden las hojas.

explanations.title: The months
explanations.body: Months are not capitalized in Spanish. Months are masculine. To say “in May”, use en mayo.

explanations.title: North and south
explanations.body: The seasons are reversed in the Southern Hemisphere. In Argentina, Chile and Uruguay, December is summer and July is winter. In Mexico and Spain the seasons are like those in the United States.

lessons.title: 102. Temperature and climate
lessons.subtitle: grados centígrados, clima seco, clima húmedo

explanations.title: Celsius, not Fahrenheit
explanations.body: In Spanish-speaking countries, as in most of the world, temperature is given in grados centígrados (degrees Celsius). To say what the temperature is, use estar a.

examples.text: Estamos a veinte grados.
examples.translation: It is twenty degrees (Celsius).

examples.text: La temperatura baja por la noche.
examples.translation: The temperature drops at night.

examples.text: Mañana la temperatura sube a treinta grados.
examples.translation: Tomorrow the temperature rises to thirty degrees.

explanations.title: Types of climate
explanations.body: Clima means the usual weather in a place over the year. It is masculine. Use ser or tener for the climate of a place, and the adjectives agree with clima.

examples.text: La costa tiene un clima templado.
examples.translation: The coast has a mild climate.

examples.text: El desierto tiene un clima muy seco.
examples.translation: The desert has a very dry climate.

explanations.title: A false friend: sensible
explanations.body: Sensible does not mean “sensible” in Spanish. It means “sensitive”. For “reasonable, sensible”, say sensato or razonable.

examples.text: Mi hermana es muy sensible.
examples.translation: My sister is very sensitive.

examples.text: Es una decisión sensata.
examples.translation: It is a sensible decision.

exercises.prompt: Which scale do Spanish-speaking countries use for the weather?
Water freezes at zero degrees Celsius. How many degrees Fahrenheit is that?
exercises.explanation: Zero degrees Celsius is thirty-two Fahrenheit.

exercises.prompt: The temperature is thirty degrees Celsius. What is the weather like?
La costa tiene un clima ___.
exercises.explanation: Clima is masculine singular, so the adjective is too.
exercises.promptTranslation: The coast has a mild climate.

exercises.prompt: Un clima ___ tiene poca lluvia.
exercises.explanation: Seco describes a climate with little rain; clima is masculine.
exercises.promptTranslation: A dry climate has little rain.

exercises.prompt: What does “sensible” mean in Spanish?
How do you say “a sensible decision”?
exercises.explanation: Sensato means sensible; decisión is feminine.

exercises.prompt: What does “La temperatura baja” mean?
How do you say “It is twenty degrees” (Celsius)?
exercises.explanation: Estar a is used with temperatures.

lessons.title: 103. Always and never: siempre, nunca
lessons.subtitle: Siempre llueve. Nunca nieva. No llueve nunca.

explanations.title: Siempre and nunca
explanations.body: Siempre means “always” and nunca means “never”. Both usually go right before the verb.

examples.text: Siempre hace frío en el invierno.
examples.translation: It is always cold in winter.

examples.text: En el desierto nunca nieva.
examples.translation: In the desert it never snows.

examples.text: Casi nunca llueve en agosto.
examples.translation: It almost never rains in August.

explanations.title: The double negative
explanations.body: In English you must not say “I don't never go”. In Spanish you must: if nunca comes AFTER the verb, put no before the verb. If nunca comes BEFORE the verb, there is no no.

explanations.title: Same family
explanations.body: The same rule works for nada (nothing) and nadie (no one): they can come after no + verb (No hay nadie) or before the verb (Nadie habla). Spanish allows several negative words in one sentence.

examples.text: No tengo nada en la maleta.
examples.translation: I have nothing in the suitcase.

examples.text: No hay nadie en la playa.
examples.translation: There is no one on the beach.

exercises.prompt: En el desierto ___ nieva.
exercises.explanation: The translation says “never”: nunca goes before the verb.
exercises.promptTranslation: In the desert it never snows.

exercises.explanation: With no before the verb, nunca after it means “never”, which matches the translation.
exercises.promptTranslation: It never rains in August.

exercises.explanation: Nunca before the verb needs no no.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is correct?

lessons.title: 104. The future tense: regular verbs
lessons.subtitle: hablaré, aprenderé, viviré

explanations.title: Add the endings to the infinitive
explanations.body: The simple future is easy: keep the whole infinitive and add the same endings to all verbs (-ar, -er and -ir): -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, -án. Every form except nosotros has a written accent.

explanations.title: Three ways to talk about tomorrow
explanations.body: Spanish can talk about the future with the present (Mañana viajo), with ir a + infinitive (Voy a viajar) or with the future tense (Viajaré). The future often sounds a bit more formal or more distant, and it is common in forecasts and predictions.

examples.text: Mañana hablaré con mi jefe.
examples.translation: Tomorrow I will talk with my boss.

examples.text: El próximo año viviremos en México.
examples.translation: Next year we will live in Mexico.

examples.text: ¿Aprenderás español pronto?
examples.translation: Will you learn Spanish soon?

examples.text: Mis amigos viajarán en diciembre.
examples.translation: My friends will travel in December.

exercises.prompt: Mañana yo ___ con el profesor.
exercises.promptTranslation: Tomorrow I will talk with the teacher.

exercises.prompt: El año próximo nosotros ___ en España.
exercises.promptTranslation: Next year we will live in Spain.

exercises.prompt: Tú ___ mucho en este curso.
exercises.promptTranslation: You will learn a lot in this course.

exercises.prompt: Mis padres ___ en diciembre.
exercises.promptTranslation: My parents will travel in December.

exercises.prompt: Ella ___ la comida mañana.
exercises.promptTranslation: She will buy the food tomorrow.

exercises.prompt: What is the future of “escribir” for yo?
Which form needs NO written accent?
exercises.explanation: Only the nosotros form has no accent.

exercises.prompt: What is the infinitive of “viviré”?
exercises.explanation: The future keeps the whole infinitive.

lessons.title: 105. The future tense: irregular stems
lessons.subtitle: tendré, saldré, haré, diré, podré

explanations.title: Twelve irregular stems
explanations.body: A few common verbs change the stem before the future endings. The endings stay the same (-é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, -án). Learn the twelve stems; they come in three groups.

rows: to have (auxiliary); habrá = there will be

explanations.title: Three groups
explanations.body: In the first group the e of the infinitive ending disappears (poder → podr-). In the second group a d replaces the vowel (poner → pondr-). Decir and hacer lose their middle letters (dir-, har-).

examples.text: Mañana tendré mucho trabajo.
examples.translation: Tomorrow I will have a lot of work.

examples.text: Mis amigos saldrán temprano.
examples.translation: My friends will leave early.

examples.text: El sábado haremos una fiesta.
examples.translation: On Saturday we will have a party.

exercises.prompt: Mañana yo ___ de la casa a las siete.
exercises.explanation: Salir has the stem saldr-: saldré.
exercises.promptTranslation: Tomorrow I will leave the house at seven.

exercises.prompt: Nosotros ___ mucho trabajo la semana próxima.
exercises.promptTranslation: We will have a lot of work next week.

exercises.prompt: Tú ___ la verdad mañana.
exercises.promptTranslation: You will tell the truth tomorrow.

exercises.prompt: Mis amigos ___ a la fiesta.
exercises.promptTranslation: My friends will come to the party.

exercises.prompt: Ella ___ la maleta en el coche.
exercises.promptTranslation: She will put the suitcase in the car.

exercises.prompt: Yo ___ ir contigo el domingo.
exercises.promptTranslation: I will be able to go with you on Sunday.

exercises.prompt: Los niños ___ jugar mañana.
exercises.explanation: Querer has the stem querr-; los niños is they.
exercises.promptTranslation: The children will want to play tomorrow.

exercises.prompt: What is the stem of “hacer” in the future?
exercises.explanation: Hacer becomes har-: haré, harás, hará.

exercises.prompt: Which infinitive gets a NEW d in its future stem?
exercises.explanation: Poner → pondr-. Poder already has a d (podr-); saber and querer just drop a vowel.

exercises.prompt: The future of “hay” (there is) is...
exercises.explanation: Haber is impersonal in the future too: habrá.

lessons.title: 106. Future weather and plans
lessons.subtitle: Mañana hará calor. Habrá tormenta. Estará nublado.

explanations.title: Today, then tomorrow
explanations.body: To turn a weather phrase into a forecast, put the verb into the future. Hace calor becomes hará calor. Hay tormenta becomes habrá tormenta (haber is always singular). Está nublado becomes estará nublado.

explanations.title: Plans for the weekend
explanations.body: The future is also useful for plans and promises. Ir a + infinitive means almost the same thing; the future sounds a little more formal.

examples.text: El sábado hará buen tiempo y iremos a la playa.

lessons.title: 107. Reading a weather forecast
lessons.subtitle: Se espera lluvia. Se acerca una tormenta.

explanations.title: The language of forecasts
explanations.body: Forecasts (informes meteorológicos) use set expressions with se. Learn them as phrases, because the verb often agrees with what is coming.

rows: Se avecina una semana de calor.
A week of heat is on the horizon.

explanations.title: Temperatures and thunder
explanations.body: Forecasts give the highest and the lowest temperature: la temperatura máxima and la temperatura mínima. They also use three words for the sounds and lights of a storm.

examples.text: La temperatura máxima será de veinticinco grados.
examples.translation: The high temperature will be twenty-five degrees.

explanations.title: A short forecast
explanations.body: Read this small forecast and notice every future form.

examples.text: Mañana habrá nubes en el norte y se esperan lluvias por la tarde.
examples.translation: Tomorrow there will be clouds in the north and rain is expected in the afternoon.

examples.text: En el sur hará sol y la temperatura máxima será de treinta grados.
examples.translation: In the south it will be sunny and the high will be thirty degrees.

examples.translation: At the weekend a cold front approaches and the temperature will drop.

lessons.title: 108. Vacation activities and places
lessons.subtitle: nadar, pescar, acampar, esquiar, caminar

explanations.title: What do you do on vacation?
explanations.body: Here are some outdoor activities. All are infinitives, so you can use them after me gusta, quiero, vamos a and similar expressions.

rows: to take a walk, to stroll

explanations.title: Where?
explanations.body: Learn the places with their articles.

lessons.title: 109. The present progressive: estar + -ando / -iendo
lessons.subtitle: Estoy estudiando. Estamos comiendo.

explanations.title: Estar plus the -ndo form
explanations.body: To say what is happening right now, use estar + the present participle (also called the gerund). Drop -ar and add -ando; drop -er or -ir and add -iendo. The -ndo form never changes: only estar does.

explanations.title: Right now, or in general?
explanations.body: The present progressive is for an action in progress, at this moment. For habits and facts use the simple present: Estudio todos los días, but Ahora estoy estudiando.

exercises.prompt: Ahora yo estoy ___ español.
exercises.promptTranslation: Right now I am studying Spanish.

exercises.prompt: Mis amigos están ___ en el restaurante.
exercises.promptTranslation: My friends are eating at the restaurant.

exercises.prompt: ¿Qué estás ___ ahora?
exercises.promptTranslation: What are you doing now?

exercises.prompt: Nosotros estamos ___ una carta.
exercises.promptTranslation: We are writing a letter.

exercises.prompt: Mi madre ___ cocinando.
exercises.promptTranslation: My mother is cooking.

exercises.prompt: Ellos ___ hablando con el jefe.
exercises.promptTranslation: They are talking with the boss.

exercises.prompt: What is the -ndo form of “vivir”?
Which sentence says what is happening NOW?
exercises.explanation: Estar + -ando shows an action in progress.

exercises.prompt: Which one is a habit rather than a right-now action?

lessons.title: 110. Irregular -ndo forms and when to use them
lessons.subtitle: leyendo, durmiendo, pidiendo, yendo

explanations.title: Between two vowels
explanations.body: If the stem of an -er or -ir verb ends in a vowel, the i of -iendo becomes y: leer → leyendo, creer → creyendo, construir → construyendo, oír → oyendo, ir → yendo.

explanations.title: -ir boot verbs change too
explanations.body: -Ir verbs with a stem change (e → ie, e → i, o → ue) also change the stem vowel in the -ndo form: dormir → durmiendo, pedir → pidiendo, decir → diciendo, seguir → siguiendo. -Ar and -er verbs normally do not (poder → pudiendo is the exception).

explanations.title: What the progressive is not for
explanations.body: In standard Spanish the progressive describes an action that is happening now. For plans use the present, ir a + infinitive or the future. Also: andar + -ndo shows an activity that goes on over a stretch of time.

examples.translation: Tomorrow I am leaving on a trip.

lessons.title: 111. Verbs followed by a + infinitive
lessons.subtitle: empezar a, comenzar a, volver a, aprender a

explanations.title: Begin, return, learn
explanations.body: Some verbs need the preposition a before an infinitive. Empezar a and comenzar a mean “to begin to”. Volver a + infinitive means to do something AGAIN: Vuelve a llover = It rains again.

rows: Empiezo a trabajar a las ocho.
Mi tía me enseña a esquiar.
Ayudo a mi madre a cocinar.

explanations.title: Boot verbs again
explanations.body: Empezar and comenzar are e → ie verbs; volver is o → ue. Nosotros and vosotros keep the original vowel.

exercises.explanation: Empezar: e → ie, and los niños is they.

lessons.title: 112. What to wear in this weather

explanations.title: Clothes for the weather
explanations.body: Link the weather and your clothes with cuando (when) and the present tense. Use hay que + infinitive for what one must do or bring in general.

uso gafas de sol y un sombrero.

explanations.title: Hay que...
explanations.body: Hay que + infinitive is impersonal: “one must” or “you have to”, for everybody. It never changes.

lessons.title: 114. My daily routine

explanations.title: From morning to night
explanations.body: Daily routines use many reflexive verbs. You can recognize them in the infinitive by the -se at the end. For now, learn them as set phrases; the next lessons explain the grammar.

explanations.title: When?
explanations.body: Add the time with a and la hora: a las siete. Use por la mañana, por la tarde and por la noche for the parts of the day, and temprano (early) or tarde (late).

lessons.title: 115. Reflexive verbs and pronouns
lessons.subtitle: me, te, se, nos, os, se

explanations.title: The action comes back to the subject
explanations.body: A reflexive verb is a verb with a reflexive pronoun: the person doing the action also receives it. In the infinitive the pronoun is the ending -se (levantarse, “to get oneself up”).

examples.text: Yo me levanto a las siete.
examples.translation: I get (myself) up at seven.

examples.text: Carmen se cepilla los dientes.
examples.translation: Carmen brushes her teeth.

examples.text: Nosotros nos bañamos después de correr.
examples.translation: We bathe after running.

explanations.title: Present tense of levantarse
explanations.body: Put the pronoun that matches the subject in front of the verb. Then conjugate the verb as usual. The pronoun is a separate word before the verb.

exercises.prompt: Yo ___ levanto a las siete.
exercises.explanation: The pronoun matches the subject: yo → me.
exercises.promptTranslation: I get up at seven.

lessons.title: 116. Where does the pronoun go?
lessons.subtitle: Me voy a levantar. Voy a levantarme. Estoy levantándome.

explanations.title: Before the verb, or attached
explanations.body: With one verb, the pronoun goes before it: Me levanto. With two verbs (a conjugated one plus an infinitive or the -ndo form), you have a choice: put the pronoun before the first verb or attach it to the end of the second one.

explanations.title: Matching and accents
explanations.body: The pronoun must always match the subject of the conjugated verb: Ellos quieren levantarse, never quieren levantarme. When a pronoun is attached to an -ndo form, add a written accent: peinando → peinándome, duchando → duchándose. With an infinitive no accent is needed.

examples.translation: They want to get up early.

examples.translation: My sister is taking a shower.

examples.text: No me quiero acostar todavía.

lessons.title: 117. Body, clothes and hygiene: use the article
lessons.subtitle: Me lavo las manos. Se pone la camisa.

explanations.title: Parts of the body
explanations.body: Learn the nouns with their articles.

explanations.title: The article, not “my”
explanations.body: With reflexive verbs, parts of the body and clothes usually take the definite article (el, la, los, las), not mi, tu or su. The pronoun already tells us whose body it is. (A possessive appears only when it adds information, as in su chaqueta nueva.)

rows: Pablo se lava la cara y las manos.
Pablo washes his face and hands.
Then he puts on his socks.

explanations.title: Things for getting ready
explanations.body: Some useful objects for personal care.

exercises.prompt: Marta se lava ___ manos.
exercises.explanation: Body parts take the article: las manos.
exercises.promptTranslation: Marta washes her hands.

exercises.prompt: Me cepillo ___ dientes después de comer.
exercises.promptTranslation: I brush my teeth after eating.

exercises.prompt: Mi hermano se pone ___ chaqueta.
exercises.explanation: Clothes also take the article, and chaqueta is feminine singular.
exercises.promptTranslation: My brother puts on his jacket.

exercises.prompt: Te lavas ___ cara todas las mañanas.
exercises.promptTranslation: You wash your face every morning.

lessons.title: 118. Reflexive verbs with stem changes
lessons.subtitle: me acuesto, me despierto, me visto

explanations.title: Boot reflexives
explanations.body: Many routine verbs are also boot verbs. The pronoun stays in front, and the verb changes as usual: acostarse (o → ue), despertarse (e → ie), vestirse (e → i), dormirse (o → ue), sentirse (e → ie).

explanations.title: More examples
explanations.body: Nosotros and vosotros keep the original vowel.

examples.text: Me despierto a las seis y me duermo a las once.
examples.translation: I wake up at six and fall asleep at eleven.

examples.text: Mis hijos se acuestan temprano.
examples.translation: My children go to bed early.

examples.translation: We get dressed and leave the house.

examples.text: Ella se siente mejor hoy.
examples.translation: She feels better today.

Which pattern does “dormirse” follow?

lessons.title: 119. Reflexive or not? Personal a
lessons.subtitle: Me lavo. Lavo la ropa. Levanto a mis hijos.

explanations.title: Same verb, different meaning
explanations.body: Many verbs can be reflexive (the action returns to you) or not (the action goes to something or someone else). When the object is a person (or a pet treated like one), add the personal a.

rows: Levanto a mis hermanos a las siete.

explanations.title: Life events
explanations.body: For these life events Spanish normally uses the reflexive: casarse (con), divorciarse (de) and mudarse (to move to a new home). To say “to die” you can use morir or morirse.

examples.text: Mi hermana se casa en junio.
examples.translation: My sister is getting married in June.

examples.text: Mis tíos se divorcian este año.
examples.translation: My aunt and uncle are getting divorced this year.

examples.text: Nos mudamos a una casa nueva.
examples.translation: We are moving to a new house.

examples.text: Mis padres se mudan a Sevilla.
examples.translation: My parents are moving to Seville.

exercises.prompt: Yo ___ a mis hermanos a las siete.
exercises.explanation: The object is people, so no pronoun and personal a.
exercises.promptTranslation: I get my brothers and sisters up at seven.

exercises.prompt: Mi madre ___ la ropa sucia.
exercises.explanation: The object is clothes: not reflexive.
exercises.promptTranslation: My mother washes the dirty clothes.

exercises.prompt: Ana ___ antes de salir.
exercises.explanation: Ana combs her own hair: reflexive.
exercises.promptTranslation: Ana combs her hair before going out.

exercises.prompt: Yo ___ a mi perro los domingos.
exercises.explanation: The dog is the object: no pronoun.
exercises.promptTranslation: I bathe my dog on Sundays.

exercises.prompt: Mis tíos ___ en junio.
exercises.explanation: Casarse with los tíos: se casan.
exercises.promptTranslation: My aunt and uncle are getting married in June.

Which verb means “to move to a new home”?
Which sentence is correct?

lessons.title: 120. Infinitive after prepositions
lessons.subtitle: sin estudiar, para jugar, cansado de nadar

explanations.title: Always the infinitive
explanations.body: After a preposition, a verb is always in the infinitive in Spanish. English often uses -ing (“tired of waiting”), but Spanish never does. This works with every preposition.

rows: Necesito una raqueta para jugar al tenis.
Con practicar mucho vas a mejorar.

explanations.title: English -ing, Spanish infinitive
explanations.body: A good rule: if the English has a preposition plus -ing, the Spanish has the same idea with the infinitive.

examples.text: Gracias por venir.
examples.translation: Thank you for coming.

lessons.title: 121. Before and after: antes de, después de
lessons.subtitle: Antes de acostarme, me lavo los dientes.

explanations.title: Antes de and después de + infinitive
explanations.body: When a verb follows antes de (before) or después de (after), it is always an infinitive in Spanish.

rows: Después de comer, descanso un poco.
After eating, I rest a little.

explanations.title: With reflexive verbs
explanations.body: If the infinitive is reflexive, the pronoun attaches to it, and it matches the subject of the sentence: antes de acostarme (I), después de ducharse (she).

examples.text: Antes de acostarme, leo un poco.
examples.translation: Before going to bed, I read a little.

examples.translation: We wash our hands before eating.

lessons.title: 122. How often? Frequency and soler
lessons.subtitle: a veces, a menudo, siempre, suelo

explanations.title: Expressions of frequency
explanations.body: These expressions say how often you do something. They usually come at the beginning or end of the sentence, and siempre, nunca and casi nunca can also go before the verb. If nunca comes after the verb, put no before the verb: No me acuesto nunca antes de las diez.

examples.text: A veces me levanto tarde los domingos.
examples.translation: Sometimes I get up late on Sundays.

examples.text: Me ducho con agua fría a menudo.
examples.translation: I often take a shower with cold water.

examples.text: Nunca me acuesto antes de las diez.
examples.translation: I never go to bed before ten.

explanations.title: Soler: to usually do
explanations.body: Soler + infinitive says what you usually do. It has no exact English equivalent: “I usually...”. It is an o → ue boot verb, and the verb after it stays in the infinitive.

examples.text: Suelo levantarme a las siete.
examples.translation: I usually get up at seven.

examples.text: ¿Qué sueles hacer después de clase?
examples.translation: What do you usually do after class?

examples.text: Solemos tomar vacaciones en el verano.
examples.translation: We usually take a vacation in the summer.

exercises.promptTranslation: I usually get up at six.

exercises.prompt: Ellos ___ salir los viernes.

exercises.prompt: ¿Qué ___ hacer tú los domingos?

lessons.title: 123. Verbs with -go: pongo, salgo, tengo, vengo
lessons.subtitle: poner, salir, tener, venir, decir, hacer, traer

explanations.title: The yo form
explanations.body: Several very common verbs have a special yo form with -go. Poner, hacer, salir, traer, caer and valer are regular in the other forms; tener, venir and decir also change their stem.

explanations.title: The full pattern
explanations.body: Tener, venir and decir are also boot verbs (e → ie or e → i), in the tú, él and ellos forms (tienes, viene, dicen). Yo has its own -go form, and nosotros and vosotros keep the e. Poner, salir, traer and caer are regular after the yo form.

exercises.prompt: Yo ___ la mochila en la silla.
exercises.promptTranslation: I put the backpack on the chair.

exercises.prompt: Yo ___ de casa a las ocho.
exercises.promptTranslation: I leave the house at eight.

exercises.prompt: Yo siempre ___ mi diccionario a clase.
exercises.promptTranslation: I always bring my dictionary to class.

exercises.prompt: Yo no ___ nada.
exercises.promptTranslation: I do not say anything.

exercises.prompt: Mis amigos ___ a mi casa los sábados.
exercises.explanation: Venir: e → ie; los amigos is they: vienen.
exercises.promptTranslation: My friends come to my house on Saturdays.

exercises.prompt: Tú ___ muchos libros a la escuela.
exercises.promptTranslation: You bring many books to school.

exercises.prompt: Ella ___ siempre la verdad.
exercises.promptTranslation: She always tells the truth.

lessons.title: 124. Salir, oír and caerse
lessons.subtitle: salir de, salir con, oír, caerse

explanations.title: Salir and its prepositions
explanations.body: Salir (to leave, to go out) is followed by different prepositions depending on what comes next.

rows: Salgo de casa a las siete.
Salgo con mis amigos los sábados.
Todo va a salir bien en el examen.

explanations.title: Oír: to hear
explanations.body: Oír has an irregular yo form (oigo) and a y in oyes, oye and oyen; oímos and oís are regular, with an accent. To get someone's attention you say oye (to a friend) or oiga (to someone you address as usted).

examples.text: Oigo la radio por la mañana.
examples.translation: I listen to the radio in the morning.

examples.text: Oiga, por favor, ¿dónde está la farmacia?
examples.translation: Excuse me, where is the pharmacy?

explanations.title: Caerse
explanations.body: Caer means to fall. When a person falls, Spanish uses the reflexive caerse. The yo form has -go: me caigo.

examples.text: Me caigo cuando patino sobre hielo.
examples.translation: I fall when I ice skate.

examples.text: Los niños se caen mucho en el parque.
examples.translation: The children fall a lot in the park.

exercises.promptTranslation: I listen to the radio in the morning.

exercises.promptTranslation: They hear the news.

lessons.title: 125. Ponerse, sentirse, estar: clothes and moods
lessons.subtitle: Me pongo nervioso. Me siento bien. Estoy contento.

explanations.title: Ponerse: put on, become
explanations.body: Ponerse has two uses. With clothes it means “to put on”. With a mood or condition it means “to get, to become”. Compare it with vestirse, which means “to get dressed” and takes no object.

rows: I get dressed in the morning.
Me pongo nervioso en los exámenes.

explanations.title: Three verbs for feelings
explanations.body: To talk about moods you can use ponerse (to get, to become), sentirse (to feel) or estar (to be). The adjective agrees with the subject: nervioso or nerviosa. Add muy or un poco to change the intensity.

examples.text: Me pongo un poco nervioso.
examples.translation: I get a little nervous.

examples.text: Los niños están muy contentos.
examples.translation: The children are very happy.

explanations.title: ¿Cómo te encuentras?
explanations.body: Encontrarse, the reflexive form of encontrar, can mean “to be, to find yourself”. It is a polite, caring way to ask how someone is doing; in everyday speech people usually just say ¿Cómo estás? (and ¿Dónde estás? instead of ¿Dónde te encuentras?)

exercises.prompt: Mi hermana se pone ___ cuando hay un examen.
exercises.promptTranslation: My sister gets nervous when there is an exam.

exercises.prompt: Los niños se ponen muy ___.
exercises.promptTranslation: The children get very happy.

exercises.prompt: Yo me ___ la chaqueta.
exercises.explanation: Ponerse takes an object: me pongo la chaqueta.
exercises.promptTranslation: I put on my jacket.

exercises.promptTranslation: Daniel gets sad when it rains.

exercises.prompt: Mi madre ___ muy cansada hoy.
exercises.promptTranslation: My mother is very tired today.

exercises.prompt: Which verb means “to feel”?

Which sentence is correct?

lessons.title: 126. Also and neither: también, tampoco
lessons.subtitle: Yo también. Yo tampoco.

explanations.title: Agreeing
explanations.body: Use también (also, too) to agree with an affirmative sentence and tampoco (neither, either) to agree with a negative one. You can answer with just Yo también or Yo tampoco.

rows: Yo también me ducho por la mañana.
No me maquillo todos los días.
Yo tampoco me maquillo todos los días.
No me maquillo todos los días.

explanations.title: Position and the double negative
explanations.body: También and tampoco can come before or after the verb. If tampoco comes after the verb, the sentence needs no before the verb, exactly like nunca.

examples.text: Yo también me levanto temprano.
examples.translation: I also get up early.

examples.text: Yo tampoco me levanto temprano.
examples.translation: I do not get up early either.

examples.text: Yo no me levanto temprano tampoco.
examples.translation: I do not get up early either.

exercises.explanation: Tampoco before the verb needs no extra no.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
exercises.explanation: After the verb, tampoco needs no before the verb.

explanations.title: A second “you”
explanations.body: In many places vos is used instead of tú, or next to it. It is the voseo. The vos verb forms are close to the vosotros forms, but without the i in -ar and -er verbs. The stress falls on the last syllable, and forms of two or more syllables have a written accent (sos, vas, ves and das do not).

explanations.title: Stem changers and irregulars
explanations.body: With vos, stem-changing verbs keep the original vowel: querés, podés, dormís, pedís. Verbs that are irregular in tú are mostly regular in vos: tenés (tienes), venís (vienes), decís (dices). Ser is sos and ir is vas.

lessons.title: 141. Ser and estar: the whole picture

explanations.title: Ser
explanations.body: Ser defines the essence of people, places and things: who they are, where they are from, what they are like and what they are made of. It is also for the time and the date.

rows: Hoy es martes. Son las diez.

explanations.title: Estar
explanations.body: Estar defines the state of people, places and things: where they are, how they feel and what condition they are in right now. It also forms the progressive.

explanations.title: The Latin roots
explanations.body: A memory aid: ser comes mainly from the Latin esse, like English “essence”. Estar comes from the Latin stare, like English “state”. Ser says what the essence is; estar says what state it is in. One exception to remember: the place of an event uses ser (La reunión es en el banco).

explanations.title: Las comidas del día
explanations.body: Most Spanish speakers eat four times a day. The big meal is often lunch, eaten in the early afternoon. The merienda is a light snack in the late afternoon, and dinner comes late and is usually lighter. The word la comida can mean “food”, “a meal” or, in some countries, “lunch”.

explanations.title: Verbs for meals
explanations.body: Each meal has its own verb: desayunar, almorzar (o → ue: almuerzo), merendar (e → ie: meriendo) and cenar. You can also say simply comer, “to eat”.

explanations.body: Use ser for what a food is like in general (its nature), and estar for how it is at this moment (temperature, taste today). With some adjectives both are possible, with a small difference.

explanations.title: Es rico, está rico
explanations.body: With ser, rico describes a general quality: a person who is rico is wealthy, and a dish that is rico is tasty by nature. With estar it says how it tastes now. To compliment the cook, say Está muy rico or Está delicioso.

explanations.body: Many words for cooking are past participles, so they work like adjectives: they change for gender and number. A menu says pollo frito, but papas fritas and carne asada.

explanations.title: Una dieta equilibrada
explanations.body: A balanced diet is una dieta equilibrada. The adjectives saludable and sano both mean “healthy”; nutritivo means “nutritious”.

lessons.title: 162. Mucho and poco: adjectives and adverbs

explanations.title: Mucho and poco as adjectives
explanations.body: When mucho or poco describes a noun, it agrees with it in gender and number: mucho, mucha, muchos, muchas (a lot of, many) and poco, poca, pocos, pocas (little, few).

explanations.title: Mucho and poco as adverbs
explanations.body: When they describe a verb, they never change: Ella come poco, Ellos trabajan mucho. Compare: Tengo mucha hambre (adjective, with hambre) and Como mucho (adverb, with the verb).

lessons.title: 163. Algo and nada

explanations.title: Positive words and their opposites
explanations.body: You already know siempre/nunca and también/tampoco. Algo (something, anything) and nada (nothing, not anything) work the same way. They do not change for gender or number.

explanations.title: Double negatives are normal
explanations.body: In Spanish, a negative word after the verb needs no before the verb: No quiero nada, No voy nunca al cine, No hablo francés y ella tampoco. If the negative word comes first, you drop no: Nunca voy al cine. Algo usually follows the verb.

lessons.title: 164. Talking about the past: time words
lessons.subtitle: ayer, anoche, la semana pasada, el año pasado

explanations.title: When did it happen?
explanations.body: Certain words tell you right away that a sentence is about a finished moment in the past. Pasado (last) is an adjective, so it agrees with its noun: la semana pasada, el año pasado.

explanations.title: The preterite: what happened?
explanations.body: Spanish has two simple past tenses, the preterite and the imperfect. In this unit you learn the preterite. It answers the question “What happened?”: an action that is finished, at a definite moment, with a clear beginning or end, or a sudden change.

explanations.title: Drop -ar, add the endings

explanations.title: In a sentence

lessons.title: 167. Nosotros: present or preterite?

explanations.title: Two tenses, one form
explanations.body: For regular -ar and -ir verbs, the nosotros form of the present and the preterite are written the same: trabajamos, vivimos, salimos. Only -er verbs differ: comemos (present) and comimos (preterite). The time word or the situation tells you which one it is.

explanations.title: Use the clues
explanations.body: Look for words like hoy, ahora and siempre (present), or ayer, anoche and el año pasado (preterite).

lessons.title: 168. The preterite of ser and ir

explanations.title: Two verbs, one preterite
explanations.body: Ser and ir are completely irregular in the preterite, and they are identical: fui, fuiste, fue, fuimos, fuisteis, fueron. None of these forms carries a written accent. The context tells you which verb it is.

explanations.title: Which verb is it?
explanations.body: Ir is usually followed by a (to a place): Fui a la playa. Ser is followed by a noun or adjective, and does not use a: Fue un día largo.

explanations.title: Life events
explanations.body: The preterite is the tense for life events: you were born once, you graduated on a definite date. Nacer is used without estar: Nací en Lima means “I was born in Lima.” Some events use a reflexive verb: graduarse, casarse, mudarse.

explanations.body: Place the reflexive pronoun before the preterite form, just like in the present: me casé, te casaste, se casó. The nosotros form is identical to the present: nos mudamos.

lessons.title: 170. Direct objects: what? whom?

explanations.title: What is a direct object?
explanations.body: The direct object is the person or thing that receives the action of the verb. To find it, ask the verb “what?” or “whom?”. In Rosa compró pan, ask: what did Rosa buy? Pan. So pan is the direct object. In Tomás llamó a sus amigas, ask: whom did Tomás call? Sus amigas.

explanations.title: Not every phrase is a direct object
explanations.body: Words that tell you where, when or how are not direct objects. In Mi madre cocinó el arroz en la cocina, the direct object is el arroz; en la cocina only says where. In Rosa compró pan ayer, ayer says when.

lessons.title: 171. Direct object pronouns: lo, la, los, las

explanations.title: Replacing the direct object
explanations.body: To avoid repeating a noun, Spanish replaces the direct object with a pronoun. The pronoun matches the noun in gender and number: Rosa compró el pan → Rosa lo compró. Tomás invitó a sus amigas → Tomás las invitó.

tables.note: Te means “you” (familiar): ¿Te llamo mañana?

explanations.title: Choosing the pronoun
explanations.body: Ask what the noun is: el pan is masculine singular → lo; la cuenta is feminine singular → la; los tacos → los; las chuletas → las. In parts of Spain, le (and les) are used instead of lo (and los) for a man or men, but lo is always correct.

lessons.title: 172. The personal a
lessons.subtitle: Visité a Roberto. Visité el museo.

explanations.title: A before a specific person
explanations.body: When the direct object is a specific person (or a pet you care about), Spanish puts the word a in front of it. This personal a has no English translation. When the object is a thing, there is no a. A + el always becomes al.

explanations.title: When there is no personal a
explanations.body: Skip the a when the person is not specific: Necesitamos un buen cocinero; Mi jefe busca gente con experiencia. Also skip it after tener: Mi vecino tiene tres perros. Common verbs that take the personal a with people: cuidar, ver, invitar, conocer, querer, amar, encontrar, ayudar.

examples.text: Ella cuidó a sus gatos.

examples.translation: We need a good cook.

lessons.title: 173. Where does the object pronoun go?
lessons.subtitle: Lo hago. Lo voy a hacer. Voy a hacerlo.

explanations.title: One verb, or a negative
explanations.body: With one verb, put the pronoun right before the conjugated verb: Ellos prepararon la ensalada → Ellos la prepararon. In a negative sentence, no goes before the pronoun: Yo no lo hago en casa.

explanations.title: Two verbs: two choices
explanations.body: With a conjugated verb plus an infinitive you may either put the pronoun before the first verb or attach it to the end of the infinitive. Both mean the same.

explanations.title: With -ando and -iendo
explanations.body: With the present progressive you can also choose. When you attach the pronoun to -ando or -iendo you add a written accent so the stress stays in the same place: está preparando → está preparándolas; está comiendo → está comiéndolo.

examples.text: Laura las está preparando.
examples.translation: Laura is preparing them.

examples.text: Laura está preparándolas.

lessons.title: 174. Answering with a pronoun in the preterite

explanations.title: Question and short answer
explanations.body: A natural answer to ¿Quién…? uses the subject, a pronoun and the preterite verb. The pronoun comes before the verb: ¿Quién preparó el menú? El cocinero lo preparó.

explanations.title: A spelling change: pagué
explanations.body: In the preterite, pagar adds a u in the yo form so that the g keeps its hard sound: yo pagué (not pagé). All the other forms are regular: pagaste, pagó, pagamos, pagaron.

explanations.title: What the waiter says and what you say
explanations.body: A waiter is a camarero (in Mexico and much of Latin America also mesero). Use usted with the staff. To ask politely, say ¿Me trae…? (literally, “do you bring me…?”). Para mí means “for me”.

explanations.title: The preterite
explanations.body: Regular -ar verbs end in -é, -aste, -ó, -amos, -asteis, -aron. Regular -er and -ir verbs end in -í, -iste, -ió, -imos, -isteis, -ieron. Ser and ir share one set of forms.

explanations.title: Objects
explanations.body: Replace the direct object with lo, la, los, las (or me, te, nos) and put it before the verb, or attach it to the infinitive. Use the personal a before a specific person. Remember algo and nada, and mucho and poco.

explanations.title: Quedar = to be located
explanations.body: Quedar is an all-purpose verb. You already know it for staying and for how clothes fit. It is also used like estar to say where a place is: ¿Dónde queda Veracruz? Veracruz queda en México.

explanations.title: Quedar a + distance
explanations.body: To say how far away a place is, use quedar a + a unit of time or distance. The unit can be hours, minutes, kilómetros or cuadras (blocks).

explanations.body: A traffic jam has many names: el embotellamiento (Argentina, Mexico, Spain, Uruguay), el atasco (Spain), el trancón (Colombia), el tapón (Puerto Rico).

lessons.title: 185. Irregular preterites: estar, tener, poder
lessons.subtitle: estuve, tuve, pude · estuvo, tuvo, pudo

explanations.title: A new stem and special endings
explanations.body: Some common verbs have an irregular stem in the preterite and a special set of endings: -e, -iste, -o, -imos, -isteis, -ieron. These endings never carry a written accent. Estar becomes estuv-, tener becomes tuv-, and poder becomes pud-.

explanations.title: Meaning
explanations.body: Tener que keeps its meaning of obligation: Tuve que esperar means “I had to wait”. Poder in the preterite often means “managed to”: Pude hablar con el piloto means “I was able to talk to the pilot”. No pude ir means “I could not go (and I didn’t)”.

lessons.title: 186. Irregular preterites: hacer, venir, decir, traer
lessons.subtitle: hice, vine, dije, traje · hizo, dijeron, trajeron · hubo

explanations.title: More irregular stems
explanations.body: These verbs use the same endings as before (-e, -iste, -o, -imos, -isteis, -ieron). The stems are hic- (hacer), vin- (venir), dij- (decir) and traj- (traer). Two details: hacer spells the él form hizo (c becomes z before o, to keep the soft sound), and after j the ending is -eron, not -ieron: dijeron, trajeron.

explanations.title: Hubo: there was, there were
explanations.body: Hubo is the preterite of haber. It means both “there was” and “there were”, and it never changes.

lessons.title: 187. Indirect objects: me, te, le, nos, les
lessons.subtitle: Mi padre me regaló un libro. Le mando el boleto.

explanations.title: To whom? For whom?
explanations.body: The indirect object tells to whom or for whom something is done: Mi padre me regaló un libro (a mí). Verbs of giving, telling, sending and showing usually have one: dar, decir, regalar, mandar, traer, comprar, vender, prestar, enseñar, mostrar.

rows: to him · to her · to you (formal) · to them · to you all
tables.note: Me, te and nos are the same as the direct object pronouns. Only the third person differs: le and les instead of lo, la, los, las.

explanations.title: Le and les, and clarifying with a
explanations.body: Le can mean to him, to her or to you (usted), and les can mean to them or to you all (ustedes). When it is not clear, add a + a name or pronoun, even though le or les is already there: Le mando el boleto a mi madre. The pronoun stays; the a-phrase only clarifies.

lessons.title: 188. The preterite of dar and ver
lessons.subtitle: di, diste, dio, dimos, dieron · vi, viste, vio, vimos, vieron

explanations.title: Dar and ver
explanations.body: Dar and ver take the regular -er/-ir endings, but because di, dio, vi and vio have only one syllable, they take no written accent (not dí, dió, ví, vió). The vosotros and ellos forms are disteis, dieron, visteis, vieron.

explanations.title: In use
explanations.body: Dar is used with indirect objects (dar un regalo a alguien) and in expressions like dar un paseo (to take a walk). Ver means to see, and it takes the personal a with people.

examples.translation: My sister gave me a gift.

lessons.title: 189. A trip told in the preterite
lessons.subtitle: El verano pasado fui a Perú con mi hermana.

explanations.title: Read the story
explanations.body: Every verb in this story is in the preterite. Find the regular forms (salimos, volamos, vimos, visitamos, comimos) and the irregular ones (fui, tuve, estuvimos, hicimos, vimos, fue).

examples.text: El verano pasado fui a Perú con mi hermana.
examples.translation: Last summer I went to Peru with my sister.

examples.text: Salimos de Miami y volamos a Lima. El viaje fue largo.
examples.translation: We left Miami and flew to Lima. The trip was long.

examples.text: Estuvimos cuatro días en Lima y hicimos muchas cosas.
examples.translation: We were in Lima for four days and did many things.

examples.text: Vimos la catedral, visitamos un museo y comimos ceviche.
examples.translation: We saw the cathedral, visited a museum and ate ceviche.

examples.translation: My sister could not walk much, but we had a great time.

explanations.title: Useful time words
explanations.body: To tell a story, start with a time marker: el verano pasado, el año pasado, hace dos años, ayer, anoche, primero, después, luego, por fin. They tell the listener that the preterite is coming.

lessons.title: 190. Hace = ago
lessons.subtitle: Llegué hace una hora. Hace dos años viajé a Lima.

explanations.title: Hace + a period of time
explanations.body: To say how long ago something happened, use the preterite and hace plus a period of time. Hace does not change, and it can come at the end or at the beginning of the sentence: Llegué hace una hora. Hace una hora llegué.

rows: El vuelo llegó hace una hora.
Compré el pasaje hace un mes.

explanations.title: More examples
explanations.body: The periods of time are plural when more than one: hace un día, hace dos días; hace una semana, hace tres semanas; hace un mes, hace seis meses; hace un año, hace diez años.

lessons.title: 191. Hace que: how long?
lessons.subtitle: ¿Cuánto tiempo hace que estudias español?

explanations.title: How long has it been?
explanations.body: The question ¿Cuánto tiempo hace que…? asks how long, and the tense of the verb tells you the meaning. With the present tense, the action is still going on: Hace dos meses que estudio español (I have been studying for two months, and I still am). With the preterite, the action is finished: Hace una hora que llegué (it has been an hour since I arrived).

rows: Hace dos meses que estudio español.
Hace un año que vivo aquí.
¿Cuánto tiempo hace que viajaste a Lima?
Hace tres años que viajé a Lima.

explanations.title: Present or preterite?
explanations.body: Ask yourself: is it still happening? If yes, use the present. If it already ended, use the preterite.

lessons.title: 192. Two object pronouns together

explanations.title: Indirect first, direct second
explanations.body: When a sentence has both an indirect and a direct object pronoun, the indirect one always comes first. A good memory aid is ID: Indirect, then Direct. Ella me dio el libro → Ella me lo dio (she gave it to me).

El camarero nos trajo las bebidas.

explanations.title: Order: me, te, nos + lo, la, los, las
explanations.body: The first pronoun (me, te, nos) tells you to whom, and the second (lo, la, los, las) tells you what. They are never separated or reversed.

lessons.title: 193. Le and les become se

explanations.title: Never “le lo”
explanations.body: Spanish does not allow le or les right before lo, la, los or las. In that position le and les both become se. So there are four possible combinations: se lo, se la, se los, se las.

rows: Se la compré en la tienda.

explanations.title: Who is “se”?
explanations.body: Se can mean to him, to her, to you (usted) or to them, so it is often clarified with a + a name or a pronoun: Se lo di a él. Se los regalé a mi hijo.

lessons.title: 194. Where double pronouns go
lessons.subtitle: Se lo voy a dar. Voy a dárselo. No se lo di.

explanations.title: Before the verb, or attached
explanations.body: Double pronouns follow the same placement rules as a single pronoun. They go before the conjugated verb, or they attach to the end of an infinitive or an -ando form. When you attach them, add a written accent so the stress stays where it was: dar → dárselo.

rows: Nicolás se lo va a alquilar.
La azafata se la está pasando.

explanations.title: Negative sentences
explanations.body: In a negative sentence, put no before the first pronoun: ¿Tus padres te compraron el boleto? No, no me lo compraron. ¿Le pasaste la maleta al empleado? No, no se la pasé.

lessons.title: 195. Gifts: who gave it to whom?
lessons.subtitle: Mi padre me lo regaló. Se la voy a regalar a mi amigo.

explanations.title: Talking about gifts
explanations.body: Gifts are a perfect place to practice double pronouns. Notice how the question and the answer fit together: the question uses nouns, and the answer replaces them with pronouns.

explanations.title: Gift ideas
explanations.body: Common gifts: un libro, una mochila, unos zapatos, una chaqueta, unos pantalones, una tarjeta, un viaje. Remember that in the third person, le and les change to se when lo, la, los or las follows.

explanations.title: Another, other
explanations.body: Otro agrees in gender and number with the noun, whether it is an adjective or stands alone as a pronoun. Never say un otro: otro already means “another”.

explanations.title: With and without the article
explanations.body: Without an article, otro means “another (one)”. With the article, el otro, la otra, los otros, las otras mean “the other one(s)”.

lessons.title: 197. The impersonal se

explanations.title: Se + verb: nobody in particular
explanations.body: When the subject is “one”, “people” or “you” in general, Spanish uses se and the third person of the verb. You see it constantly on signs, ads, announcements and instructions. The verb agrees with the thing: singular noun → singular verb (Se vende casa), plural noun → plural verb (Se venden casas).

explanations.title: In everyday talk
explanations.body: The impersonal se also describes customs and general facts: A las cinco de la tarde se toma el té. ¿Cuánta fruta se necesita para una dieta equilibrada?

explanations.title: Typical notices
explanations.body: Notices are short and use the impersonal se. Learn the patterns, and you will understand most of the signs you see on the street.

explanations.title: Patterns
explanations.body: Se vende / se venden = for sale. Se alquila / se alquilan = for rent. Se necesita = wanted, needed. Se ofrece = offered. Se prohíbe = forbidden. Se habla = spoken.

lessons.title: 199. A history of the railroad

explanations.title: Read the story
explanations.body: Histories use the preterite for events that started and ended. Read this short history of a railroad. Find the regular verbs and the irregular ones.

explanations.body: When the stem of an -er or -ir verb ends in a vowel, the i of the ending becomes y in the él and ellos forms: construir → construyó, construyeron; leer → leyó, leyeron; creer → creyó, creyeron.

lessons.title: 200. Review: travel, irregular preterites and object pronouns
lessons.subtitle: Fuimos, tuve, hace dos años, se lo di, otro boleto, se vende

explanations.title: Irregular preterites at a glance
explanations.body: Special stems take the special endings -e, -iste, -o, -imos, -isteis, -ieron (with no accents). After j the ending is -eron. Ser and ir share forms, and dar and ver use regular -er/-ir endings with no accent.

explanations.title: Other tools from this unit
explanations.body: Hace + time = ago. Hace + time + que + present or preterite tells how long. In a double pronoun, the indirect one comes first and le/les become se before lo, la, los, las. Otro never takes un. The impersonal se appears on signs.

explanations.title: Places to stay
explanations.body: El alojamiento (also el hospedaje) is the general word for lodging. The verbs alojarse and hospedarse both mean to stay somewhere. In many Spanish-speaking families, a vacation means visiting relatives and staying at their house, so the family often hosts people for weeks.

explanations.body: For international travel you often need papers: el pasaporte, la visa, el acta de nacimiento (birth certificate), la licencia de manejar (driver’s license), el comprobante (receipt, proof). La vigencia is how long a document is valid, and la cuota is a fee.

explanations.title: Three more irregular stems
explanations.body: These verbs use the same endings as estar, tener and poder (-e, -iste, -o, -imos, -isteis, -ieron), with no written accents. The stems are pus- (poner), sup- (saber) and quis- (querer).

explanations.title: The meaning changes in the preterite
explanations.body: Saber in the preterite means “found out”: Ayer supe la noticia. Querer in the preterite means “tried” (Quise abrir la puerta); No quise means “I refused”. Poner means “put” or “placed”.

lessons.title: 207. Irregular preterites: andar, -ucir and compounds
lessons.subtitle: anduve, conduje, traduje, detuve

explanations.title: Andar and the -ucir verbs
explanations.body: Andar becomes anduv- and follows the pattern of estar and tener. All verbs ending in -ucir (conducir, traducir, producir, reducir, introducir) use the stem -duj- and take -eron in the ellos form, like decir.

explanations.title: Compounds keep the irregularity
explanations.body: A verb built on an irregular verb keeps the irregularity: tener → detener (detuve, detuvo), mantener (mantuve), obtener (obtuve); poner → posponer (pospuse); hacer → deshacer (deshice); traer → contraer (contraje).

lessons.title: 208. Spelling changes in the yo preterite

explanations.title: Keeping the sound
explanations.body: Verbs ending in -car, -gar and -zar change their spelling in the yo form of the preterite, so that the last consonant keeps the sound of the infinitive. Every other form is regular.

explanations.title: Only the yo form changes
explanations.body: Compare: yo busqué, tú buscaste, él buscó. The tú, él, nosotros and ellos forms keep the original consonant because the following vowel (a or o) does not change the sound.

explanations.title: When the i would sit between vowels
explanations.body: In -er and -ir verbs whose stem ends in a vowel (caer, oír, leer, creer, construir), the ending -ió becomes -yó, and -ieron becomes -yeron. This only happens in the él and ellos forms. The other forms need a written accent on the í: caí, caíste, caímos.

explanations.title: In use
explanations.body: Caerse is often used for things that fall: Se cayó la maleta. Oír means to hear and also to listen (with attention). Leer and creer you already know in the present.

lessons.title: 210. Stem-changing -ir verbs in the preterite

explanations.title: Only -ir verbs, only él and ellos
explanations.body: In the present, boot verbs change in many forms. In the preterite, -ar and -er verbs have no stem change at all. Only -ir verbs change, and only in the él/ella/usted and ellos/ellas/ustedes forms: e → i and o → u. The other four forms use the regular stem.

explanations.title: Common verbs
explanations.body: e → i: pedir, servir, seguir, repetir, conseguir, vestirse, sugerir, mentir (mintió), sentir (sintió), preferir, divertirse. o → u: dormir (durmió), morir (murió).

lessons.title: 213. Formal commands: usted and ustedes

explanations.title: How to form a formal command
explanations.body: A command tells someone what to do. Formal commands are used with people you address as usted (one person) or ustedes (more than one). Take the yo form of the present tense, drop the -o, and add the opposite vowel: -ar verbs take -e / -en, and -er and -ir verbs take -a / -an.

explanations.title: Using commands politely
explanations.body: Add por favor to be polite. The pronouns usted and ustedes may follow the command for emphasis or clarity: Escriba usted la dirección. In writing, a strong command can sit between exclamation marks.

lessons.title: 214. Formal commands: irregular and stem-changing verbs

explanations.title: Start from the yo form
explanations.body: The rule still works for irregular yo forms, because the command copies the yo form: pongo → ponga, hago → haga, vengo → venga. Stem-changing verbs keep the change in the command: duermo → duerma, pido → pida, pienso → piense.

explanations.title: Spelling changes and the truly irregular ones
explanations.body: Verbs ending in -car, -gar and -zar change their spelling, as in the preterite, so that the sound stays: buscar → busque, llegar → llegue, cruzar → cruce. Dar, ir, ser, estar and saber are fully irregular. Dé (from dar) has a written accent to tell it from the preposition de.

lessons.title: 221. Review: lodging, the preterite and commands

explanations.title: The preterite patterns
explanations.body: Regular: habló, comió, vivió. Irregular stems: estuve, puse, supe, quise, anduve, conduje, hice, vine, dije, traje. Fui for both ser and ir. Spelling changes in the yo form: busqué, llegué, empecé. Y-change: cayó, leyó, oyeron. Stem changes in -ir verbs (él and ellos only): pidió, durmieron.

explanations.title: Formal commands
explanations.body: Take the yo form, drop -o, add the opposite vowel (-e / -en for -ar; -a / -an for -er and -ir). Keep the stem change and the irregular yo form. Dar, ir, ser, estar and saber are irregular. Put no in front for a negative command.

lessons.title: 223. What do I do with it? Pronouns in recipes
lessons.subtitle: ¿Qué hago con los frijoles? Hay que dejarlos en agua.

explanations.title: Asking and answering about ingredients
explanations.body: When you ask ¿Qué hago con…? and the answer repeats the noun, use a direct object pronoun instead. With an expression plus an infinitive (tienes que, debes, necesitas), the pronoun can go before the first verb or attach to the infinitive. With hay que the pronoun can only attach to the infinitive: Hay que cocinarlo.

rows: Las debes freír en una sartén.

explanations.title: Both positions work
explanations.body: Los tienes que dejar and Tienes que dejarlos mean the same thing. When you attach the pronoun to the infinitive, no accent is needed on a regular infinitive (dejarlos, cortarla), but freír needs it: freírlos.

explanations.title: El Día de los Reyes Magos
explanations.body: In many Spanish-speaking countries children receive gifts on January sixth, el Día de los Reyes Magos. The traditional treat is the rosca de Reyes, a ring-shaped bread with a small figure of the baby Jesus baked inside. Whoever finds the figure must host a party on February second, el Día de la Candelaria (traditionally with tamales).

lessons.title: 226. Verbs like gustar
lessons.subtitle: Me gusta la música. Le encantan los regalos. Te molesta el ruido.

explanations.title: The thing liked is the subject
explanations.body: Gustar and similar verbs work backwards from English: the thing that pleases is the subject, and the person is an indirect object (me, te, le, nos, les). So the verb agrees with the thing, not the person. Singular thing or an infinitive → gusta; plural thing → gustan.

explanations.title: Who is it about?
explanations.body: Add a + a name or pronoun for emphasis or clarity: A mí me gusta la música. A mi hermana le encanta bailar. A nosotros nos molesta el ruido. Make it negative with no before the pronoun: No me gusta esperar.

explanations.title: Hundreds, thousands and years
explanations.body: Hundreds agree in gender with the noun (doscientas personas, doscientos dólares). Mil never takes -s and is not preceded by un: mil dólares, dos mil dólares. Years are read as whole numbers: dos mil veinte; mil novecientos noventa.

explanations.title: Numbers in real situations
explanations.body: Flight numbers, room numbers, prices and years all use these patterns. Some countries separate the thousands with a period (1.250) and others with a comma (1,250); years are never separated.

lessons.title: 232. Unit review: travel, lodging and commands
lessons.subtitle: Fuimos, pidió, hace dos años · Siga derecho, no fume

explanations.title: What to remember
explanations.body: Travel stories use the preterite: regular endings, special stems (tuve, puse, supe, quise, anduve, conduje, hice, vine, dije, traje), fui for ser and ir, spelling changes in yo (busqué), the y-change (cayó, leyó) and stem changes in -ir verbs (pidió, durmieron). Hace + time = ago. Directions and signs use formal commands.

rows: Siga derecho y doble a la izquierda.

explanations.title: Putting it together
explanations.body: A traveler asks for directions, and a hotel clerk answers with commands. Both talk about what happened using the preterite.

examples.text: Ayer llegué al hotel y pedí una habitación con vista al mar.
examples.translation: Yesterday I arrived at the hotel and asked for a room with an ocean view.

examples.text: Hace dos días mis padres me dieron los boletos. Me los dieron en el aeropuerto.
examples.translation: Two days ago my parents gave me the tickets. They gave them to me at the airport.

examples.text: Señor, salga del hotel, siga derecho y doble a la derecha.
examples.translation: Sir, leave the hotel, go straight and turn right.

exercises.promptTranslation: My parents gave me the tickets. They gave them to me at the airport.

options: I have been arriving for an hour.
