options: General facts based on official counts

lessons.title: 677. Reading: Spain, the Canary Islands and the sea route
lessons.subtitle: Las personas que cruzan el mar arriesgan su vida; los equipos de rescate intentan salvarlas.

explanations.title: A dangerous crossing
explanations.body: This reading summarizes general facts from news reports and organizations. It does not give routes or tips for crossing, and it does not describe the experience of any individual.

examples.text: España está en el sur de Europa y recibe a personas que llegan por tierra, por mar y por aire.
examples.translation: Spain is in the south of Europe and receives people who arrive by land, by sea and by air.

examples.text: En los últimos años, muchas personas han llegado a las Islas Canarias en embarcaciones pequeñas, como pateras y cayucos.
examples.translation: In recent years many people have arrived in the Canary Islands in small boats, such as pateras and cayucos.

examples.text: El viaje por el océano Atlántico es muy peligroso, y organizaciones humanitarias informan de muchas muertes.
examples.translation: The trip across the Atlantic Ocean is very dangerous, and humanitarian organizations report many deaths.

examples.text: El servicio de Salvamento Marítimo rescata a muchas personas que están en peligro en el mar.
examples.translation: The Maritime Rescue service rescues many people who are in danger at sea.

examples.text: Los gobiernos discuten cómo organizar la acogida y cómo proteger las fronteras al mismo tiempo.
examples.translation: Governments debate how to organize reception and how to protect borders at the same time.

examples.text: Algunas organizaciones piden rutas legales y seguras para que nadie tenga que arriesgar su vida.
examples.translation: Some organizations ask for legal and safe routes so that nobody has to risk his or her life.

examples.text: Otras personas piden más controles para que haya menos salidas en barco.
examples.translation: Other people ask for more controls so that fewer boats depart.

exercises.prompt: What are “pateras” and “cayucos”?

options: It rescues people in danger at sea

options: Because the sea is too small

lessons.title: 678. Reading: the Venezuelan exodus and the region
lessons.subtitle: Millones de venezolanos han salido de su país, y la mayoría vive en América Latina.

explanations.title: A regional movement of people
explanations.body: This reading summarizes how international organizations describe the situation. Opinions about the causes differ, and the text says who holds each view.

examples.text: Según organismos internacionales, millones de venezolanos han salido de su país en los últimos años.
examples.translation: According to international organizations, millions of Venezuelans have left their country in recent years.

examples.text: La mayoría vive en otros países de América Latina y el Caribe, como Colombia, Perú, Ecuador y Chile.
examples.translation: Most live in other Latin American and Caribbean countries, such as Colombia, Peru, Ecuador and Chile.

examples.text: Varias organizaciones y gobiernos mencionan la crisis económica, la inflación y los problemas políticos.
examples.translation: Several organizations and governments mention the economic crisis, inflation and political problems.

examples.text: El gobierno de Venezuela rechaza algunas críticas y dice que las sanciones económicas causaron parte de la crisis.
examples.translation: The Venezuelan government rejects some criticism and says that economic sanctions caused part of the crisis.

examples.text: Los países que reciben a los migrantes necesitan escuelas, hospitales y empleos para todos.
examples.translation: The countries that receive the migrants need schools, hospitals and jobs for everyone.

examples.translation: Some governments give residence permits so that people can work legally.

examples.translation: Many communities help the newcomers, although sometimes there are also tensions.

lessons.title: 679. Reading: remittances and families across borders
lessons.subtitle: Muchos migrantes envían dinero a sus familias para que puedan comer, estudiar y vivir mejor.

explanations.title: Money that crosses borders
explanations.body: A remesa is the money that a migrant sends to relatives in the country of origin. In several countries, remittances are an important part of the economy.

examples.text: Una remesa es el dinero que un migrante envía a sus parientes en su país de origen.
examples.translation: A remittance is the money that a migrant sends to relatives in his country of origin.

examples.text: Muchos migrantes envían dinero cada mes para que su familia pueda comer, estudiar y pagar el alquiler.
examples.translation: Many migrants send money every month so that their family can eat, study and pay the rent.

examples.text: En algunos países, las remesas son una parte importante de la economía.
examples.translation: In some countries, remittances are an important part of the economy.

examples.text: Las empresas de transferencias y los bancos cobran una comisión por enviar el dinero.
examples.translation: Transfer companies and banks charge a fee for sending the money.

examples.text: Algunos expertos dicen que las remesas ayudan a reducir la pobreza.
examples.translation: Some experts say that remittances help reduce poverty.

examples.text: Otros dicen que no resuelven los problemas de fondo y que hacen falta empleos en el país de origen.
examples.translation: Others say that they do not solve the underlying problems and that jobs are needed in the country of origin.

lessons.title: 680. Feelings on a long journey: esperanza, miedo, nostalgia, dignidad
lessons.subtitle: Extraño a mi familia, pero tengo esperanza.

explanations.title: Words for strong feelings
explanations.body: Many stories about migration use words of emotion. Learn these to read and talk about them with respect.

rows: Tengo esperanza de una vida mejor.
Sentí miedo cuando salí de casa.
Todas las personas merecen vivir con dignidad.
La despedida llenó la casa de tristeza.
Después del viaje, el cansancio era enorme.
La soledad es difícil al principio.

explanations.title: Two ways to say “to miss”
explanations.body: In Latin America, extrañar is the most common verb for “to miss someone.” In Spain, echar de menos is the usual phrase; it is also understood in Latin America. Be careful: extrañar a alguien means to miss someone, but un lugar extraño means a strange place.

examples.text: Extraño a mi familia, pero tengo esperanza.
examples.translation: I miss my family, but I have hope.

examples.text: Echo de menos a mis amigos del pueblo.
examples.translation: I miss my friends from the town.

examples.text: Un nudo en la garganta le impidió hablar.
examples.translation: A lump in his throat kept him from speaking.

What does “la nostalgia” mean?
options: A longing for home or the past

lessons.title: 681. Everyday expressions: echar un vistazo, hacer caso, probar suerte, darse cuenta
lessons.subtitle: Echa un vistazo a la lista. Hazme caso. Quiero probar suerte en otra ciudad.

explanations.title: Phrases that are used as one unit
explanations.body: These expressions are common in conversation. Learn each as a block, because the words do not translate one by one.

to pay attention to, to listen to
Quiero probar suerte en otra ciudad.
Me di cuenta de que faltaba un documento.
Hay que tener en cuenta el costo.
El proyecto se pone en marcha en enero.

lessons.title: 682. Building an argument: first, also, however, in conclusion
lessons.subtitle: En primer lugar, hay que escuchar a todos. Sin embargo, también hay que pensar en el costo.

explanations.title: Linking words for an opinion
explanations.body: A clear argument has an order. These connectors make it easy to follow.

explanations.title: A balanced paragraph

lessons.title: 683. Review: adverbial clauses, all conjunctions

explanations.title: One chart for all
explanations.body: Purpose and condition conjunctions (para que, antes de que, sin que, a menos que, con tal de que, en caso de que) always take the subjunctive. Time conjunctions (cuando, en cuanto, tan pronto como, después de que, hasta que) take the subjunctive for future or pending actions and the indicative for habits and the past. Aunque takes the indicative for a fact and the subjunctive for a possibility.

rows: para que, antes de que, sin que
a menos que, con tal de que, en caso de que
cuando, en cuanto, hasta que, después de que
future → subjunctive; habit or past → indicative

explanations.title: Three kinds of clauses
explanations.body: Noun clauses follow a verb of wish, emotion, doubt or denial (quiero que vengas). Adjectival clauses describe a noun and take the subjunctive when the noun is unknown or does not exist (busco a alguien que venga). Adverbial clauses begin with a conjunction (te espero hasta que vengas).

lessons.title: 693. Forming the imperfect subjunctive: trabajara, comiera, viviera
lessons.subtitle: Mi jefe quería que yo trabajara más. Mis padres querían que viviéramos cerca.

explanations.title: Three steps
explanations.body: 1. Take the ellos form of the preterite (trabajaron, comieron, vivieron). 2. Drop -ron (trabaja-, comie-, vivie-). 3. Add -ra, -ras, -ra, -ramos, -rais, -ran. The endings are the same for -ar, -er and -ir verbs. The nosotros form has a written accent on the vowel before -ramos.

tables.note: Yo and él forms are identical, as in the present subjunctive.

explanations.title: When is it used?
explanations.body: The imperfect subjunctive is used in a que clause when the main verb is in a past tense (preterite, imperfect, pluperfect) or the conditional: quería que, pedí que, necesitaba que, esperaría que.

examples.translation: My boss wanted me to work more hours.

With the ellos form of the preterite

lessons.title: 694. Irregular imperfect subjunctive: fuera, tuviera, pudiera, hiciera, dijera
lessons.subtitle: Si yo fuera tú… Quería que tuvieras paciencia y que dijeras la verdad.

explanations.title: Irregular preterite, irregular subjunctive
explanations.body: Any verb with an irregular ellos form in the preterite carries the same stem into the imperfect subjunctive. The endings stay regular: -ra, -ras, -ra, -áramos or -iéramos, -rais, -ran.

exercises.promptTranslation: My mother wanted me to have more patience.

Which is the imperfect subjunctive of ser for ellos?

lessons.title: 695. Stem-changing and -yeron verbs: pidiera, durmiera, creyera, construyera
lessons.subtitle: Pidieron que durmiéramos. Era posible que creyeran la noticia.

explanations.title: Same stem as the preterite ellos form
explanations.body: -ir stem-changing verbs change in the ellos form of the preterite (pidieron, durmieron, sintieron, siguieron), so that stem appears in every person of the imperfect subjunctive. Verbs whose stem ends in a vowel use y: creyeron, leyeron, construyeron, oyeron, cayeron.

exercises.promptTranslation: My parents asked us to sleep early.

exercises.prompt: El gerente quería que yo ___ el contrato esa tarde.
exercises.promptTranslation: The manager wanted me to read the contract that afternoon.

exercises.prompt: Era posible que ellos ___ la noticia sin dudar.
exercises.promptTranslation: It was possible that they believed the news without doubting.

exercises.prompt: La empresa pidió que los ingenieros ___ la fábrica en un año.
exercises.promptTranslation: The company asked the engineers to build the factory in a year.

exercises.prompt: Mi jefe quería que yo ___ su carro a la oficina.

exercises.promptTranslation: It was sad that nobody heard the neighbors’ complaints.

exercises.promptTranslation: The workers asked the company to give them more money.

exercises.prompt: Which is the imperfect subjunctive of pedir for yo?
Which is the imperfect subjunctive of sentir for ellos?

lessons.title: 696. The second set of endings: hablase, tuviese, pidiésemos
lessons.subtitle: Mi madre quería que yo estudiase / estudiara.

explanations.title: -ra or -se: same meaning
explanations.body: The imperfect subjunctive has two sets of endings that mean the same thing. Both are formed from the ellos form of the preterite: -se, -ses, -se, -semos, -seis, -sen. The -ra forms are more common in Latin America; the -se forms are common in writing and in Spain. The nosotros form takes a written accent in both sets.

tables.note: Use whichever form you hear most. Either one is correct.

explanations.title: Same sentence, two forms
explanations.body: Both sentences below mean exactly the same thing.

examples.text: Mi madre quería que yo estudiara.
examples.translation: My mother wanted me to study.

examples.text: Mi madre quería que yo estudiase.
examples.translation: My mother wanted me to study.

exercises.promptTranslation: My mother wanted me to study more.

exercises.explanation: More frequent in Spain and in writing.

lessons.title: 697. In the past: wishes and requests (quería que, pedí que, necesitaba que)
lessons.subtitle: Mis padres querían que estudiara. El jefe pidió que llegáramos temprano.

explanations.title: Past trigger → imperfect subjunctive
explanations.body: When the main verb of a wish, request, command or preference is in the past, the verb in the que clause goes into the imperfect subjunctive. Compare: Quiero que estudies. (present) → Quería que estudiaras. (past).

exercises.prompt: Mis padres querían que yo ___ en la universidad.
exercises.promptTranslation: My parents wanted me to study at the university.

exercises.prompt: El jefe pidió que todos ___ temprano ese lunes.
exercises.promptTranslation: The boss asked everyone to arrive early that Monday.

exercises.prompt: Necesitábamos que alguien nos ___ con la mudanza.
exercises.promptTranslation: We needed somebody to help us with the move.

exercises.prompt: Los trabajadores exigieron que la empresa les ___ un aumento.
exercises.promptTranslation: The workers demanded that the company give them a raise.

exercises.prompt: Mi abuela prefería que nosotros ___ en su casa.
exercises.promptTranslation: My grandmother preferred that we eat at her house.

exercises.prompt: Ayer mi hermano me pidió que lo ___ al aeropuerto.
exercises.promptTranslation: Yesterday my brother asked me to take him to the airport.

exercises.prompt: Hoy mi hermano me pide que lo ___ al aeropuerto.
exercises.promptTranslation: Today my brother asks me to take him to the airport.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is correct?

Quería que venir a la reunión.
Quería que vengas a la reunión.

exercises.prompt: Why is “Pedí que llegaran” in the imperfect subjunctive?
options: The main verb is in the past

lessons.title: 698. In the past: emotions (me sorprendió que, temía que, me molestó que)
lessons.subtitle: Me sorprendió que ninguno de sus partidarios se acercara. Temía que no termináramos a tiempo.

explanations.title: Reacting to a past event
explanations.body: After a past emotion verb, the verb that follows (with a different subject) goes into the imperfect subjunctive. If the verb in the first clause is a preterite such as me sorprendió, the second verb can refer to a moment before or at the same time as the surprise.

rows: Me alegro de que estés aquí.
Me alegré de que estuvieras aquí.
tables.note: Sentir que = to be sorry that; sentir = to feel is different.

exercises.promptTranslation: I was afraid that they wouldn’t finish on time.

exercises.promptTranslation: It bothered the director that the employees said that.

exercises.promptTranslation: I was glad that you were at the party that day.

exercises.promptTranslation: It outraged all of us that the government spent so much money.

exercises.promptTranslation: I was worried that the company would fire so many workers.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is correct?

lessons.title: 699. In the past: doubt, denial and impersonal expressions
lessons.subtitle: Dudaba que vinieran. Negó que hubiera problemas. Era importante que todos supieran la verdad.

explanations.title: Doubt, denial and value judgments in the past
explanations.body: Dudar que and negar que stay in the subjunctive and move to the imperfect subjunctive when the main verb is in the past. Impersonal expressions such as era importante que, era necesario que and era extraño que also take it. Statements of certainty (estaba seguro de que, sabía que) take the indicative; no dudaba que usually does too, because the speaker is certain.

rows: Es extraño que no digan nada.
Era extraño que no dijeran nada.

exercises.prompt: Dudaba que ellos ___ a la reunión.
exercises.promptTranslation: I doubted that they would come to the meeting.

exercises.prompt: El presidente negó que ___ problemas en la economía.

exercises.prompt: Era importante que todos ___ la verdad.

exercises.prompt: Era extraño que ella no ___ nada.
exercises.promptTranslation: It was strange that she said nothing.

exercises.prompt: No dudaba que ellos ___ a la reunión; siempre venían.
exercises.promptTranslation: I didn’t doubt that they came to the meeting; they always came.

exercises.prompt: Era necesario que los obreros ___ un contrato nuevo.
exercises.promptTranslation: It was necessary for the workers to sign a new contract.

exercises.prompt: Dudábamos que el gobierno ___ resolver la crisis.
exercises.promptTranslation: We doubted that the government could solve the crisis.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence expresses certainty about the past?
options: Estaba seguro de que ellos venían.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is correct?

lessons.title: 700. Sequence of tenses: present subjunctive or imperfect subjunctive?
lessons.subtitle: Quiero que vengas. Quería que vinieras.

explanations.title: The main verb sets the tense
explanations.body: The tense of the main verb decides which subjunctive follows. Present, future, present perfect and commands usually lead to the present subjunctive. Preterite, imperfect and conditional lead to the imperfect subjunctive.

exercises.prompt: Dile que ___ a la reunión mañana.
exercises.promptTranslation: Tell him to come to the meeting tomorrow.

exercises.promptTranslation: I would like you to come with me.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
Which sentence is correct?

lessons.title: 701. In the past: describing something unknown or nonexistent
lessons.subtitle: Buscaba un empleo que pagara bien. No había nadie que supiera la respuesta.

explanations.title: Adjectival clauses in the past
explanations.body: The same rule you learned in Unit 31 applies. If the person or thing was unknown or did not exist, use the imperfect subjunctive after a past main verb. If the person or thing existed, use the indicative.

rows: Buscaba un empleo que pagara bien.
Tenía un empleo que pagaba bien.
No había nadie que supiera la respuesta.
Había alguien que sabía la respuesta.
Necesitaba un socio que tuviera dinero.
Conocí a un socio que tenía dinero.
No conocía a nadie que viviera allí.
Conocía a varias personas que vivían allí.

exercises.promptTranslation: I met a worker who worked in that factory.

lessons.title: 702. In the past: para que, antes de que, sin que, en caso de que, cuando
lessons.subtitle: Trabajó mucho para que sus hijos estudiaran. Dijo que me llamaría cuando llegara.

explanations.title: Adverbial clauses after a past main verb
explanations.body: Para que, antes de que, sin que and en caso de que usually take the imperfect subjunctive when the main verb is in the preterite or imperfect and the action is seen from that past moment. A menos que usually follows a conditional main verb (Dijo que no iría a menos que lo invitaran). Time conjunctions follow the same logic: a completed past action takes the indicative (Cuando llegó, cenamos), but a future-in-the-past takes the imperfect subjunctive (Dijo que me llamaría cuando llegara).

rows: Trabajó mucho para que sus hijos estudiaran.
Salimos antes de que empezara la lluvia.
Entró sin que nadie lo viera.
Llevé dinero en caso de que lo necesitara.
Dijo que me llamaría cuando llegara.

exercises.promptTranslation: My father worked hard so that his children could study.

exercises.prompt: Salimos antes de que ___ la lluvia.
exercises.promptTranslation: We left before the rain started.

exercises.promptTranslation: She entered the building without anyone seeing her.

exercises.prompt: Llevé dinero en caso de que lo ___.
exercises.explanation: En caso de que + imperfect subjunctive.
exercises.promptTranslation: I took money in case I needed it.

exercises.promptTranslation: He said he would call me when he arrived.

lessons.title: 703. Polite requests: quisiera, pudiera, debiera
lessons.subtitle: Quisiera un café, por favor. ¿Pudiera usted ayudarme?

explanations.title: A softer way to ask
explanations.body: The imperfect subjunctive of querer, poder and deber makes a request or an opinion more polite. Quisiera is very common in shops, restaurants and offices. Quiero is direct; quisiera is softer.

tables.note: Pudiera and debiera are formal and more common in writing and in some regions. In speech, many people use the conditional (podría, debería).

explanations.title: In a shop or an office
explanations.body: These are typical polite sentences.

examples.text: Quisiera una mesa para cuatro personas, por favor.
examples.translation: I would like a table for four people, please.

examples.text: Quisiéramos hablar con el director.
examples.translation: We would like to speak with the director.

examples.text: ¿Pudiera decirme dónde está la oficina de información?

lessons.title: 704. Wishes and comparisons: ojalá + imperfect subjunctive, como si
lessons.subtitle: Ojalá tuviera más tiempo. Habla como si fuera el dueño.

explanations.title: Wishes that are unlikely or unreal; comparisons that are untrue
explanations.body: Ojalá + imperfect subjunctive expresses a wish that is unlikely or contrary to the present reality. Como si + imperfect subjunctive means “as if” and is used for something untrue or imagined. Compare: Ojalá tenga tiempo mañana (a real possibility) / Ojalá tuviera tiempo (but I don’t have it).

rows: I wish I had more time. (I don’t.)
I wish we could travel together.
Habla como si fuera el dueño.
He talks as if he were the owner. (He isn’t.)
Me trata como si no supiera nada.
She treats me as if I knew nothing.
I hope I have time tomorrow. (It is possible.)

lessons.title: 705. More verbs that work like gustar: convenir, costar, bastar, importar, tocar
lessons.subtitle: Me conviene vender ahora. Me cuesta levantarme temprano. Basta con una firma.

explanations.title: The gustar pattern: the thing or action comes after the verb
explanations.body: These verbs follow the pattern of gustar: an indirect object pronoun (me, te, le, nos, les) shows who is affected, and the verb agrees with the thing or action that comes after.

rows: It is in my interest to sell now.
It is in our interest to wait.
It is hard for me to get up early.
The price doesn’t matter to me.
Hoy me toca pagar a mí.
Today it’s my turn to pay.

explanations.title: Present and past
explanations.body: Convenir behaves like venir (it conviene, convenía, convino). Costar changes o → ue (cuesta, cuestan).

lessons.title: 706. Reading: the maquiladora model
lessons.subtitle: Una maquiladora ensambla productos para exportar.

explanations.title: Factories that assemble for export
explanations.body: A maquiladora (or maquila) is a factory that assembles products, often with imported parts, and sends them to another country to be sold. They are common in northern Mexico and in parts of Central America. People disagree about their effects, and this reading gives the main arguments.

lessons.title: 707. Reading: one product, many countries
lessons.subtitle: Un teléfono puede tener piezas hechas en diez países.

explanations.title: The supply chain
explanations.body: A global product often passes through many hands before it reaches the store. The chain of companies and countries that makes a product is called la cadena de suministro. Consumers can usually see only the price and the label.

examples.text: Un teléfono puede tener piezas hechas en muchos países diferentes.

explanations.title: A country that has debated its model
explanations.body: Chile is often cited in debates about economic models. This reading summarizes what supporters and critics say, and the facts that are widely reported.

lessons.title: 710. Awareness: human trafficking and how to get help
lessons.subtitle: La trata de personas es un delito grave: una persona es engañada o forzada para ser explotada.

explanations.title: A serious crime and a human-rights issue
explanations.body: This lesson explains what human trafficking is at a general level, so that people can recognize it and know where to seek help. It does not describe how traffickers operate. La trata de personas (human trafficking) is different from the smuggling of migrants: in trafficking, the person is exploited through deception, threats or force, even when they traveled voluntarily at first.

examples.text: La trata de personas es un delito grave en casi todos los países.
examples.translation: Human trafficking is a serious crime in almost all countries.

examples.translation: Victims can lose their freedom and not receive the promised pay.

examples.text: Algunas señales de alerta son que alguien no puede salir libremente o no tiene sus propios documentos.
examples.translation: Some warning signs are that someone cannot leave freely or does not have his or her own documents.

examples.text: Si usted sospecha que alguien es víctima de trata, avise a las autoridades o a una línea de ayuda de su país.
examples.translation: If you suspect that someone is a victim of trafficking, notify the authorities or a help line in your country.

examples.text: Muchos países tienen leyes para castigar la trata y proteger a las víctimas.
examples.translation: Many countries have laws to punish trafficking and protect the victims.

examples.translation: Civil organizations offer shelter, medical help and legal help to victims.

lessons.title: 713. Review: the imperfect subjunctive in all its main uses
lessons.subtitle: Quería que viniera. Buscaba a alguien que supiera. Salió sin que lo vieran. Ojalá pudiera.

explanations.title: Five uses at a glance
explanations.body: 1. After a past wish, request, emotion, doubt or denial: Quería que viniera. 2. In a description of an unknown or nonexistent thing in the past: Buscaba a alguien que supiera. 3. After conjunctions of purpose and contingency in the past: Salió sin que lo vieran. 4. For unreal wishes and comparisons: Ojalá pudiera. Habla como si fuera el jefe. 5. For polite requests: Quisiera un café.

explanations.title: Two related rights
explanations.body: Freedom of expression is the right of every person to share opinions and information. Freedom of the press is the right of the media to investigate and publish without being controlled by the government. Both are protected by international law and by many constitutions, but countries limit them in different ways.

explanations.title: What societies try to do
explanations.body: After dictatorships or armed conflicts, many countries try to deal with the past in several ways. Specialists often name four main goals: truth, justice, reparation and guarantees that it will not happen again. Many countries also add memory as a related goal. Countries combine them in different ways, and people disagree about the best balance.

examples.translation: Reparation: helping the victims and their families, for example with economic or psychological support.

examples.text: La memoria: museos, monumentos y días de recuerdo para que la sociedad no olvide.
examples.translation: Memory: museums, monuments and days of remembrance so that society does not forget.

explanations.title: Choosing the tenses
explanations.body: Spanish has three main patterns with si. (1) A real or likely situation: si + present indicative, followed by the present, the future or a command. (2) An imaginary or unlikely situation: si + imperfect subjunctive, followed by the conditional. (3) A habit in the past: si + imperfect indicative, followed by the imperfect.

Si tienes tiempo, ven a visitarme.
Si estudias mucho, pasas el examen.
Si lloviera mañana, nos quedaríamos en casa.
Si yo fuera presidente, construiría más escuelas.
Cuando era niño, si llovía, nos quedábamos en casa.

lessons.title: 731. Imaginary questions: ¿Qué harías si…?

lessons.title: 732. Reading: what would change? Arguments about rights
lessons.subtitle: Si no existiera la libertad de prensa, sería más difícil conocer los problemas.

explanations.title: Arguments with if-clauses
explanations.body: People who defend rights often use imaginary situations to explain why a right matters. The sentences below are arguments that people make, not proven facts, and other people may disagree with them.

examples.text: Si no existiera la libertad de prensa, sería más difícil conocer los problemas del gobierno.
examples.translation: If freedom of the press did not exist, it would be harder to learn about the government’s problems.

examples.text: Si los trabajadores no tuvieran sindicatos, tendrían menos poder para negociar.
examples.translation: If workers did not have unions, they would have less power to negotiate.

examples.text: Si hubiera más escuelas accesibles, más niños con discapacidad estudiarían con sus compañeros.
examples.translation: If there were more accessible schools, more children with disabilities would study with their classmates.

examples.text: Si la policía registrara todos los casos, sabríamos mejor cuántos delitos de odio hay.
examples.translation: If the police recorded all cases, we would know better how many hate crimes there are.

examples.text: Muchos expertos creen que habría menos pobreza si todos los niños pudieran ir a la escuela.
examples.translation: Many experts believe there would be less poverty if all children could go to school.

examples.text: Si las lenguas indígenas se enseñaran en las escuelas, más niños las conservarían.
examples.translation: If Indigenous languages were taught in schools, more children would keep them.

examples.text: Otras personas responden que, además de una ley, también haría falta aplicarla.
examples.translation: Other people answer that, besides a law, it would also be necessary to apply it.

exercises.prompt: Why is the reading using imaginary situations?
options: To explain why a right matters

exercises.prompt: Are the sentences presented as proven facts?
options: No, they are arguments people make

options: It would be necessary to apply it

lessons.title: 733. Review: adjectival clauses, known or unknown, present and past
lessons.subtitle: Busco un abogado que sepa de derechos humanos. No había nadie que hablara árabe.

explanations.title: Indicative or subjunctive?
explanations.body: After a noun, use the indicative when the person or thing exists and is known. Use the subjunctive when it is unknown, may not exist, or does not exist (nadie, ninguno, cualquiera). In past contexts, the subjunctive is the imperfect subjunctive.

Busco un abogado que sepa de derechos humanos.
No hay nadie que sepa la respuesta.
Cualquiera que conozca la ley debe acatarla.
En el pueblo no había ninguna escuela que tuviera ascensor.
No había nadie que hablara árabe.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence describes a person who may not exist?

Conozco a un abogado que sabe de derechos humanos.
Mi abogado sabe de derechos humanos.
Tengo un abogado que sabe de derechos humanos.

Which sentence is correct?

lessons.title: 734. Review: adverbial clauses, always subjunctive or future vs habit
lessons.subtitle: Antes de que empiece, sin que lo sepan, a menos que llueva. Cuando llegue, te llamo.

explanations.title: Two groups of conjunctions
explanations.body: Group 1 always takes the subjunctive: para que, antes de que, sin que, a menos que, con tal de que, en caso de que. Group 2 takes the subjunctive for a future or pending event but the indicative for a habit or a fact: cuando, en cuanto, tan pronto como, después de que, hasta que, aunque.

rows: Voy a hablar con ellos antes de que empiece la reunión.
Saldremos mañana a menos que llueva.
Mañana, cuando llegue a casa, te llamaré.
Todos los días, cuando llego a casa, descanso.
Aunque llueva mañana, iremos al parque.
Salió sin que nadie lo viera.

explanations.title: Softening an opinion
explanations.body: The conditional makes an opinion sound careful and polite. It is common in debates, interviews and reports. Useful frames: yo diría que…, me parecería…, sería mejor…, no estaría de acuerdo con…, podríamos…

explanations.title: Choosing the pattern
explanations.body: Likely: si + present, … present, future or command. Imaginary or unlikely: si + imperfect subjunctive, … conditional. Past habit: si + imperfect, … imperfect. The conditional also expresses politeness, advice, a future seen from the past and a guess about the past.

explanations.title: Choosing mood after conjunctions
explanations.body: Always subjunctive: para que, antes de que, sin que, a menos que, con tal de que, en caso de que. Subjunctive for the future, indicative for habit or past: cuando, en cuanto, después de que, hasta que. Aunque takes the indicative for a known fact and the subjunctive for something hypothetical or unknown. Porque and como (because) take the indicative.

explanations.body: Take the ellos form of the preterite, remove -ron, and add -ra, -ras, -ra, -ramos (with an accent on the vowel before), -rais, -ran. Irregular preterite stems carry over: dijeron → dijera; fueron → fuera; tuvieron → tuviera; leyeron → leyera; vinieron → viniera.

lessons.title: 758. World organizations: ONU, OMS, UNESCO and CEPAL
lessons.subtitle: La ONU trabaja por la paz y la seguridad del mundo.

explanations.title: Four organizations you hear about in the news
explanations.body: These organizations appear often in news about international affairs. The descriptions are short summaries, not complete definitions.

rows: La ONU trabaja por la paz y la seguridad del mundo; su sede está en Nueva York.
La OMS se ocupa de la salud en todo el mundo; su sede está en Ginebra.

La UNESCO apoya la educación, la ciencia y la cultura; su sede está en París.
the UN commission for Latin America and the Caribbean
La CEPAL estudia la economía de América Latina y el Caribe; su sede está en Santiago de Chile.

explanations.title: Useful phrases
explanations.body: Use tener su sede en to say where an organization has its headquarters, and ser miembro de to say that a country belongs to it.

lessons.title: 759. More organizations: Banco Mundial, INTERPOL, OPEP and OTAN
lessons.subtitle: INTERPOL ayuda a las policías de muchos países a compartir información.

explanations.title: Four more names
explanations.body: These four organizations have very different jobs. Notice the verbs in the examples: ayudar, prestar, compartir, exportar.

rows: El Banco Mundial presta dinero y da apoyo a países en desarrollo; su sede está en Washington.
INTERPOL ayuda a las policías de muchos países a compartir información; su sede está en Lyon.
La OPEP reúne a países que exportan petróleo; su sede está en Viena.
La OTAN es una alianza militar de defensa colectiva; su sede está en Bruselas.

explanations.title: What each one does not do
explanations.body: Do not mix up their jobs. INTERPOL is not an army: it helps police forces share information. The OTAN is a military alliance, but the Banco Mundial is a bank for development. According to the treaty of the OTAN, an attack on one member is treated as an attack on all, and each member agrees to help, taking the action it considers necessary.

lessons.title: 760. Diplomacy: embajador, canciller, cumbre, tratado
lessons.subtitle: El canciller y el embajador hablan con otros gobiernos sobre un tratado.

explanations.title: People and documents
explanations.body: El canciller is the foreign minister in many Latin American countries. El embajador represents a country in another country. A tratado, an acuerdo, a convenio and a pacto are all agreements, but tratado sounds the most formal.

rows: El canciller viaja a la cumbre.
La embajadora habla con el ministro del país vecino.
En la cumbre, los presidentes hablan de comercio.
Los dos países firman un tratado.
Los dos gobiernos llegan a un acuerdo.
Ese convenio protege a los trabajadores migrantes.
Estos países tienen una alianza económica.

explanations.title: Gender of the nouns
explanations.body: El canciller and el embajador change for women: la canciller and la embajadora. The nouns tratado, acuerdo, convenio and pacto are masculine; la cumbre and la alianza are feminine.

examples.text: La embajadora firmó el convenio.
examples.translation: The ambassador (f.) signed the agreement.

lessons.title: 761. Verbs of treaties: ratificar, estipular, entrar en vigor
lessons.subtitle: El tratado entra en vigor cuando el Congreso lo ratifica.

explanations.title: From signing to taking effect
explanations.body: First, two governments negociar (negotiate) and acordar (agree on) something. Then they firmar the treaty. In many countries the congress must ratificar it. The text estipula (stipulates) the rules, and the treaty entra en vigor (takes effect) on a certain date.

rows: Los gobiernos acuerdan un plazo de cinco años.
El texto estipula las reglas del comercio.
El tratado entra en vigor en enero.
Un país impone una sanción a otro.
Los dos países amplían el acuerdo.

explanations.title: The present tense of acordar and imponer
explanations.body: Acordar changes o → ue (acuerdo, acuerdas, acuerda, acordamos, acordáis, acuerdan). Imponer has an irregular yo form (impongo) and is otherwise regular (impones, impone, imponemos, imponéis, imponen).

explanations.title: Words for talking about trade
explanations.body: These words appear in news about trade agreements and foreign debt.

El comercio de bienes es muy importante.
La fábrica compra insumos en el extranjero.

explanations.title: Hedging in economic news
explanations.body: Reports about the economy often use words like según (according to), algunos, otros and creen que because experts do not always agree. In the examples below, notice how they avoid saying that something is certain.

lessons.title: 763. Regional organizations and trade agreements
lessons.subtitle: Argentina, Brasil, Paraguay y Uruguay fundaron el Mercosur.

explanations.title: Five regional names
explanations.body: Latin American and Caribbean countries have created several regional organizations. These are only a few of them.

explanations.title: What is a free-trade agreement?
explanations.body: A tratado de libre comercio (TLC) lowers or removes tariffs between the countries that sign it. Its defenders say that it increases trade and creates jobs. Its critics say that it can hurt some workers or industries. Economists do not always agree about the results.

lessons.title: 765. Sanctions and sovereignty: two points of view
lessons.subtitle: Algunos gobiernos imponen sanciones; otros dicen que violan su soberanía.

explanations.title: Words for a debate
explanations.body: A sanción is a measure that one government or group of governments imposes on another to put pressure on it. Sanctions are controversial. Notice the words that mark different opinions: según (according to), algunos, otros, dicen que.

rows: Un gobierno puede sancionar a empresas o a personas.
Algunos dicen que las sanciones perjudican a la población.
Un gobierno puede decir que otro socava su soberanía.
La soberanía es el poder de un país para decidir sobre su territorio.
Una injerencia es entrar en los asuntos de otro país.
Los expertos discuten el alcance de las sanciones.

explanations.title: Both sides
explanations.body: Governments that impose sanctions usually say that they want to press another government to change its policy. Governments that receive sanctions often say that sanctions are illegal or unfair. Experts disagree about how well sanctions work and whom they affect most.

lessons.title: 767. The United States and Latin America: a long and complex relationship

explanations.title: “Nuestra América”
explanations.body: In the nineteenth century, the Cuban writer José Martí published an essay titled “Nuestra América”. Today people still use the phrase when they talk about regional identity, and different writers read it in different ways.

explanations.title: Adjectives from the news
explanations.body: Reports about foreign affairs use these adjectives often. Adjectives ending in -o change for gender and number (duradero, duradera, duraderos, duraderas); most adjectives ending in -e, -l or -z only change for number (confiable, confiables; bilateral, bilaterales; feliz, felices). Adjectives of nationality that end in a consonant, and those ending in -or, add -a for the feminine (español, española; trabajador, trabajadora).

explanations.title: The same verb, a different meaning
explanations.body: Adding se (me, te, nos…) can change a verb’s meaning a little or a lot. You do not need to memorize every pair now; learn to notice the pronoun and let the context help you.

explanations.title: Present tense with the pronoun

explanations.title: Four forms of government
explanations.body: These are simple definitions. Real governments often mix features, and political scientists describe them in more detail.

rows: En una democracia, los ciudadanos eligen a sus gobernantes en elecciones libres.
En una república, el jefe del Estado no es un rey; ocupa el cargo por un tiempo limitado.
En una monarquía, un rey o una reina es la cabeza del Estado.
En una dictadura, una persona o un grupo pequeño tiene el poder sin límites claros.

explanations.title: Two kinds of monarchy
explanations.body: In an absolute monarchy, the monarch’s power has no limits set by another authority. In a constitutional monarchy, a constitution limits the monarch’s power, and elected officials usually govern. A democracy can exist in a republic or in a constitutional monarchy.

lessons.title: 782. Aristocracia, oligarquía, tiranía, demagogia
lessons.subtitle: Una oligarquía es un gobierno de un grupo pequeño que defiende sus intereses.

explanations.title: Four more words
explanations.body: These four words describe forms of government or political strategies. They are often used critically.

rows: La aristocracia es una clase privilegiada formada por la nobleza o por familias muy ricas.
En una oligarquía, un grupo pequeño concentra el poder y defiende sus propios intereses.
Una tiranía es un gobierno que usa el poder de forma cruel o injusta.
La demagogia busca apoyo con promesas fáciles y apelando a las emociones, no a la razón.

explanations.title: A classical idea
explanations.body: An old idea from ancient Greek philosophers says that each good form of government can degenerate into a bad one. In one version of this scheme, monarchy can become tyranny and aristocracy can become oligarchy; some authors add that rule by the people can degenerate into rule by the mob, led by demagogues. Modern scholars use the idea as a starting point, not as a complete theory.

explanations.title: Separation of powers
explanations.body: Many democracies divide the power of the state into three branches. The idea is to create a balance, so that no single branch has too much power.

lessons.title: 785. Ideologies and economic systems: capitalismo, socialismo, marxismo
lessons.subtitle: Cada ideología tiene defensores y críticos.

explanations.title: Short definitions
explanations.body: These definitions are simplified. Each word has many versions, and people often disagree about their meaning and their results. Notice how the text attributes opinions to defenders and critics.

rows: El capitalismo se basa en la propiedad privada y en el mercado.
El socialismo defiende un papel mayor del Estado y más igualdad; existen versiones muy diferentes.
El comunismo propone que los medios de producción sean comunes.
El marxismo parte de las ideas de Karl Marx y Friedrich Engels y critica el capitalismo.
El liberalismo defiende la libertad individual y limita el poder del Estado.
Hay un monopolio cuando una sola empresa controla un mercado.

explanations.title: Defenders and critics
explanations.body: Defenders of capitalism say that it creates wealth and encourages innovation. Critics say that it can increase inequality. Defenders of socialism say that it can reduce inequality. Critics say that too much state control can reduce freedom and efficiency. Economists and voters disagree.

lessons.title: 786. Democracy in Latin America: transitions and discontent
lessons.subtitle: En la segunda mitad del siglo veinte, varios países pasaron de gobiernos autoritarios a democracias.

explanations.title: A general picture
explanations.body: Historians and political scientists often describe the last decades of the twentieth century as a time of transitions from authoritarian governments to democracies in several Latin American countries, especially in South America. Today, according to several surveys, many citizens are not satisfied with how democracy works, but support for democracy as an idea remains high in many countries. The picture differs from country to country.

examples.text: En la segunda mitad del siglo veinte, varios países pasaron de gobiernos autoritarios a democracias.
examples.translation: In the second half of the twentieth century, several countries moved from authoritarian governments to democracies.

examples.translation: The situation is different in each country.

explanations.title: Two meanings of democracy
explanations.body: Some authors say that democracy has two levels: it is a political system (with elections and the vote) and it is also a way of life (respect, participation, ethics). When both levels fail, citizens may feel discontent.

lessons.title: 787. Colonies, independence and self-determination
lessons.subtitle: La autodeterminación es el derecho de un pueblo a decidir su futuro político.

explanations.title: Key words
explanations.body: These words are used in history and in political news.

La descolonización es el proceso por el que una colonia llega a gobernarse a sí misma.

La autodeterminación es el derecho de un pueblo a decidir su futuro político.
Un territorio puede tener un gobierno propio con poderes limitados.

explanations.title: The United Nations and decolonization
explanations.body: The United Nations has a committee that studies territories that do not yet govern themselves fully, and it keeps an official list of them. Each year the committee also discusses the question of Puerto Rico, although Puerto Rico is not on that list and the United States considers the matter an internal one. People in Puerto Rico and outside it hold different opinions about its political future: some prefer statehood, some prefer independence, and some prefer to keep the present status.

lessons.title: 795. Simón Bolívar and the idea of “bolivarianismo”
lessons.subtitle: Simón Bolívar es llamado “el Libertador” en varios países de América del Sur.

explanations.title: A historical figure and a political label
explanations.body: Simón Bolívar was born in Caracas and fought for the independence of several territories in South America. He is a national hero in several countries and is known as “el Libertador”. Bolívar dreamed of a close union among the new republics, though that union did not last. He died in the year eighteen thirty.

explanations.title: What is “bolivarianismo”?
explanations.body: Bolivarianismo is a general name for ideas inspired by Bolívar, such as regional unity and independence. Different leaders and movements have used his name at different times and with different meanings. Some defenders say that it expresses a tradition of regional unity. Some critics say that today the name is sometimes used to support current political goals. Historians often remind us that Bolívar lived in a very different time.

examples.translation: Many politicians cite historical figures to support their ideas.

lessons.title: 796. The “marea rosa”: shifts to the left and to the right
lessons.subtitle: Los politólogos llaman “marea rosa” a una ola de gobiernos de izquierda en América Latina.

explanations.title: A term used by journalists and scholars
explanations.body: The expression “marea rosa” (pink tide) refers to the wave of left and center-left governments that were elected in several Latin American countries, starting around the end of the nineteen nineties and the beginning of the two thousands. The name “pink” (rather than “red”) is usually explained by the fact that many of those governments were moderate. Later, voters in several countries elected governments of the right, and in recent years the political map has changed again.

examples.translation: Political scientists discuss whether the term is useful, because the governments were very different.

explanations.title: Words for describing change
explanations.body: A giro is a turn. An ola is a wave. An alternancia (alternation) happens when different parties win power in different elections. A giro a la izquierda means a turn toward the left, and a giro a la derecha means a turn toward the right.

lessons.title: 797. Populism: a debated word
lessons.subtitle: Populismo es un término muy discutido: los expertos no están de acuerdo.

explanations.title: Definitions differ
explanations.body: Scholars do not agree on a single definition of populism. Many describe it as a political style or strategy that divides society into “el pueblo” and “las élites” and claims to speak for the people. Critics say that populist leaders make easy promises and weaken institutions. Defenders say that populism gives a voice to people whom traditional parties ignore. There are populists of the left and of the right, and politicians often use the word as an insult against their opponents.

examples.translation: Critics say that populist leaders make easy promises.

examples.translation: Defenders say that it gives a voice to people whom traditional parties ignore.

examples.translation: Politicians often use the word as an insult against their opponents.

explanations.title: Words around populism
explanations.body: La retórica is the use of language to persuade. La oratoria is the art of public speaking. Un orador is a speaker. Un demagogo is a person who wins support with easy promises and emotional appeals. Una élite is a small group with a lot of power or influence.

lessons.title: 798. Disinformation and freedom of expression: a balanced debate
lessons.subtitle: Algunas personas quieren regular la desinformación; otras temen que eso limite la libertad de expresión.

explanations.title: Two concerns
explanations.body: False information can spread very fast on social media. Some people ask for laws that limit it, and others worry that those laws could be used to silence opinions. Both groups say that they want to protect society. Below are arguments that people make, not proven facts.

Las mentiras pueden causar daño real.
Es mejor educar a la gente y verificar los datos.

explanations.title: Other ideas
explanations.body: Some people prefer solutions that do not restrict speech: teaching media literacy, supporting independent journalists, and making platforms explain how their systems work. Each person can weigh these ideas and form their own opinion.

lessons.title: 799. Review: present perfect and pluperfect
lessons.subtitle: He terminado el informe. Ya habían terminado cuando llegué.

explanations.title: How to form the perfect tenses
explanations.body: Both tenses use haber + a past participle. The participle never changes after haber. For the present perfect, haber is in the present (he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, han). For the pluperfect, haber is in the imperfect (había, habías, había, habíamos, habíais, habían). The pluperfect tells what had already happened before another moment in the past.

rows: Había puesto las llaves en la mesa.

explanations.title: Usage note
explanations.body: In Spain, people use the present perfect often for things that happened recently (Hoy he comido temprano). In much of Latin America, the preterite is often used for the same idea (Hoy comí temprano). Both are correct in their regions.

examples.text: Cuando llegué, ya habían terminado.
examples.translation: When I arrived, they had already finished.

lessons.title: 800. Perfect tenses with estar and an adjective: ha estado preocupado

explanations.title: How someone has been feeling
explanations.body: To say what state someone has been in, use haber + estado + an adjective. The adjective agrees in gender and number with the subject. The word estado itself never changes. Because we describe how someone is feeling or doing (a state or condition), we use estar and not ser.

explanations.title: Something has been done by someone
explanations.body: To say that something has been done or had been done (usually by someone else), use haber + sido + a participle. The participle agrees with the thing that received the action. Add por to name the person who did it.

explanations.title: Ser or estar?
explanations.body: Han sido firmados means that someone signed the documents (an action). Están firmados means that the documents are in a signed state (a result). Spanish also has a passive with se: Se han firmado los documentos.

lessons.title: 802. Perfect continuous: han estado hablando, había estado leyendo
lessons.subtitle: Los vecinos han estado hablando con los técnicos durante semanas.

explanations.title: An action in progress up to a moment
explanations.body: Use haber + estado + a gerund (-ando, -iendo) for an action that has been going on for a while. The present perfect continuous (han estado hablando) connects the action to now. The past perfect continuous (habían estado hablando) connects it to an earlier moment in the past.

explanations.title: Gerunds and pronouns
explanations.body: Gerunds of -er and -ir verbs with a vowel before the ending use -yendo (leer → leyendo). Some stem-changing -ir verbs change the vowel (dormir → durmiendo, pedir → pidiendo). A pronoun goes before haber or attached to the gerund (with a written accent): Lo han estado discutiendo = Han estado discutiéndolo.

examples.translation: They have been discussing it for weeks.

lessons.title: 803. The present perfect subjunctive: espero que hayas llegado
lessons.subtitle: Me alegra que hayan aprobado la ley. Espero que hayas llegado bien.

explanations.title: Haya + participle
explanations.body: The present perfect subjunctive is haber in the present subjunctive (haya, hayas, haya, hayamos, hayáis, hayan) + a past participle. Use it when a trigger for the subjunctive (emotion, doubt, hope, denial) is followed by something that has already happened.

rows: Me alegra que hayan aprobado la ley.

explanations.title: English speakers
explanations.body: In English you often use the simple past in these sentences (“I hope you arrived safely”). In Spanish, the completed action is usually expressed with the present perfect subjunctive: Espero que hayas llegado bien. The main verb is in the present, in the future, or a command.

lessons.title: 804. Present perfect subjunctive after cuando, en cuanto, hasta que
lessons.subtitle: Te llamaré en cuanto haya terminado. Cuando hayas llegado a la esquina, dobla a la derecha.

explanations.title: Completed before another future moment
explanations.body: After time words like cuando, en cuanto, tan pronto como, después de que and hasta que, use the subjunctive when the action has not happened yet. When you want to stress that it will be completed first, use haya + participle. The main verb is future, a command, or a similar reference to the future.

explanations.title: Past or future?
explanations.body: Compare: Cuando llegué, llamé (past, indicative). Cuando haya llegado, llamaré (future, subjunctive). In many sentences, the simple present subjunctive is also possible: Te llamaré en cuanto termine.

lessons.title: 805. Doubt and probability about the past: dudo que haya, es posible que hayan

explanations.title: Not sure about the past
explanations.body: To doubt or to guess about something that may have already happened, use a trigger + que + haya + participle.

rows: Dudo que el tren haya salido.
No creo que ellos hayan firmado.
Es posible que ya hayan firmado el acuerdo.
Es probable que haya llovido en la noche.
Quizás haya perdido las llaves. (The indicative is also possible when you feel more sure.)

explanations.title: Subjunctive or indicative?
explanations.body: Use the subjunctive after doubt: Dudo que haya salido. Use the indicative after belief or certainty: Creo que ha salido. With no creo que, the subjunctive returns.

lessons.title: 807. Reading: a town meeting about water (invented)

explanations.title: An invented story
explanations.body: This short text is invented for practice. It does not describe a real place. Notice the perfect tenses: han estado preocupados, había prometido, no ha publicado, haya cumplido, hayan encontrado, hayan terminado.

lessons.title: 827. The conditional perfect: habría comido

explanations.title: How to form the conditional perfect
explanations.body: The conditional perfect means “would have + participle.” Build it with haber in the conditional (habría, habrías, habría, habríamos, habríais, habrían) + a past participle. The participle never changes. It is the same participle that you use in the present perfect and the pluperfect.

rows: Ella habría ido a la fiesta.

explanations.title: Quick contrast
explanations.body: The simple conditional says what would happen (comería = I would eat). The conditional perfect says what would have happened earlier (habría comido = I would have eaten).

explanations.title: Probably, in the past
explanations.body: Spanish uses the conditional perfect to guess about something that probably happened before a past moment. It works like “must have” or “probably had” in English. The guess is about an earlier event. Native speakers often add words like probablemente or seguramente, but the tense itself already shows the guess.

explanations.title: A note about use
explanations.body: This use is less common than other ways of guessing, and you will see it more in writing, but you may also hear it in conversation. Many speakers also use probablemente + the pluperfect or the preterite.

lessons.title: 830. The pluperfect subjunctive: hubiera comido, hubiese comido

explanations.title: How to form it
explanations.body: The pluperfect subjunctive uses haber in the imperfect subjunctive + a past participle. Like the imperfect subjunctive, it has two forms: the -ra forms (hubiera) and the -se forms (hubiese). Both mean the same thing. It is used mostly after si when you imagine something in the past that did not happen, and after expressions of wish or regret.

explanations.title: A first look at use
explanations.body: The most common pattern is si + pluperfect subjunctive, then the conditional perfect. You will practice it in the next lessons.

The clause with si can come first or second. In an if-clause that imagines the past, do not use habría right after si; use hubiera or hubiese.

explanations.title: Order of the clauses

explanations.title: A different past, a different present
explanations.body: Sometimes an imagined past event would change how things are now. In that case, the si-clause uses the pluperfect subjunctive (past), and the result clause uses the simple conditional (present). Words like ahora and todavía show that the result belongs to the present.

explanations.title: Pattern at a glance

lessons.title: 833. Speaking naturally: hubiera in both halves, hubiese and habría
lessons.subtitle: Si lo hubiera sabido, hubiera ido. Si lo hubiese sabido, habría ido.

explanations.title: What you will hear
explanations.body: In this kind of si-clause (imagined past), only the pluperfect subjunctive is standard (hubiera or hubiese). In the result clause, careful and written Spanish uses habría + participle. In speech, many people use hubiera + participle in the result clause too (Si lo hubiera sabido, hubiera ido). You will hear this a lot, but in formal writing prefer habría.

explanations.title: Hubiera or hubiese?
explanations.body: There is almost no difference between them. Hubiera is more common in many places, and hubiese sounds a little more formal or literary. Pick one and use it consistently.

lessons.title: 834. Three kinds of si-sentences: real, imagined now, imagined past

explanations.title: One idea, three levels of reality
explanations.body: Spanish si-sentences change their verbs depending on how real the situation is. Real or likely things use the indicative. Imagined things in the present or future use the imperfect subjunctive and the conditional. Imagined things in the past use the pluperfect subjunctive and the conditional perfect.

explanations.title: Never after si
explanations.body: In conditional si-clauses, do not use the present subjunctive, the future or the conditional after si. (In indirect questions such as No sé si vendrá, si can take the future.) The only subjunctive forms after si are the imperfect (estudiara) and the pluperfect (hubiera estudiado).

explanations.title: How magical realism works
explanations.body: In magical realism, a strange event, such as a person rising into the sky, is described in a calm voice. The characters are not shocked. The effect is that the reader accepts the extraordinary as part of daily life. Many critics link this to oral storytelling, in which grandparents tell wonders in a serious tone.

explanations.title: Three famous authors
explanations.body: These short portraits are in our own words. Julio Cortázar (1914–1984), born in Belgium to Argentine parents, is known for short stories where the fantastic breaks into daily life, and for the novel Rayuela (1963), which readers can enter in different orders. Jorge Luis Borges (1899–1986), from Buenos Aires, wrote short stories, essays and poems about libraries, mirrors, labyrinths and infinity; Ficciones is one of his best-known books. Isabel Allende, a Chilean writer born in Lima in 1942, became widely known for La casa de los espíritus (1982), a family saga with some magical elements. Her books have been translated into many languages.

explanations.title: Using the preterite and present perfect
explanations.body: Use the preterite for the moment a work was written. The present perfect is often used for something that still holds today (in much of Latin America, the preterite or the present is also common).

explanations.title: About these words

explanations.title: Nine verbs

Aquejar is usually used in the third person and often as a participle: aquejado de = suffering from.

to ignore; to be unaware of

explanations.title: Fourteen verbs
explanations.body: Most are regular. Verbs ending in -car or -gar change spelling before e in the yo form of the preterite: inculcar → inculqué, recalcar → recalqué, prolongar → prolongué.

explanations.body: Tergiversar is a formal verb that suggests dishonesty. Galardonar is mostly used in news about prizes, usually in the passive: fue galardonado con el premio.

explanations.body: An aphorism is a short sentence that expresses a general idea. The sayings below were written for this course. They are not famous quotations. Read each aloud and then read its meaning.

explanations.title: As if…
explanations.body: Como si means “as if” or “as though.” It introduces a comparison with something imaginary or doubtful. After como si, use the subjunctive: the imperfect subjunctive for something happening at the same time as the main verb (whether the main verb is in the present or the past), and the pluperfect subjunctive for something earlier (see the next lesson).

explanations.title: Notes
explanations.body: In this meaning, do not use the present indicative or the conditional after como si. The subject of the como si-clause can be the same as the main subject or different. Como si is always written as two words.

explanations.body: When the imagined situation comes before the main verb, use como si + the pluperfect subjunctive (hubiera + participle). If the imagined situation happens at the same time, use the imperfect subjunctive.

explanations.title: Two kinds of ojalá
explanations.body: Ojalá means “I hope” or “I wish.” It always takes the subjunctive. With the present subjunctive it expresses a hope that could come true. With the imperfect subjunctive it expresses a wish for something unlikely or impossible now. Que after ojalá is optional.

rows: Ojalá viviéramos cerca de la playa.

explanations.title: Translating
explanations.body: In English the first group sounds like “I hope.” The second group sounds like “I wish.” The speaker uses the imperfect subjunctive to show distance from reality.

lessons.title: 859. Ojalá + pluperfect subjunctive: regrets about the past
lessons.subtitle: Ojalá hubiera estudiado más. Ojalá hubieras venido a la fiesta.

explanations.title: I wish it had been different
explanations.body: To wish that the past had been different, use ojalá + the pluperfect subjunctive (hubiera + participle). It expresses regret, and it cannot be changed.

I wish they had arrived on time.
I wish it had not rained so much.

explanations.title: What not to say
explanations.body: Do not use habría after ojalá. Do not use the indicative either. Hubiera (or hubiese) is the only normal choice.

lessons.title: 860. Quisiera: politeness and wishes

explanations.title: A softer way to say “I want”
explanations.body: Quisiera is the imperfect subjunctive of querer (-ra form). It sounds more polite than quiero. You will hear it in restaurants, shops and offices. It can also express a wish about what you would like to do or see happen.

explanations.title: Same subject or different subject?
explanations.body: If the subject is the same in both clauses, use quisiera + infinitive. If the subjects are different, use quisiera que + the imperfect subjunctive.

Quisiera que mi hermano estudiara más.

explanations.title: Choosing the right form
explanations.body: Match the verb form to the type of wish. A hope that is likely uses the present subjunctive. A wish about an unlikely present situation uses the imperfect subjunctive. A regret about the past uses the pluperfect subjunctive. A polite wish or a wish about another person uses quisiera or me gustaría que + imperfect subjunctive.

Ojalá no hubiéramos perdido el tren.

explanations.title: A quick check
explanations.body: Ask yourself: Is it possible or likely? Is it about now or about the past? Is it about me or about someone else? The answers choose the form.

lessons.title: 862. Review: the pluperfect subjunctive in si, ojalá and como si
lessons.subtitle: Si hubiera ido… Ojalá hubiera ido… Habló como si hubiera ido…

explanations.title: Three triggers, one form
explanations.body: The pluperfect subjunctive (hubiera / hubiese + participle) appears after si, ojalá and como si when the situation is imagined and in the past. It always has the same shape.

rows: Si hubiera salido antes, habría llegado.
If I had left earlier, I would have arrived.
I wish I had left earlier.
Habla como si hubiera salido antes.
He talks as if he had left earlier.

explanations.title: What to remember
explanations.body: In the main clause after a si-clause, use the conditional perfect (habría + participle); in speech hubiera + participle is also possible. After ojalá and como si there is no conditional. The participles are the same as in the other perfect tenses: hecho, dicho, escrito, visto, vuelto.

lessons.title: 864. Review: ser, estar and haber in a story of the past (a railroad)
lessons.subtitle: El trabajo era duro. Los trabajadores estaban lejos de su familia. Hubo accidentes.

explanations.title: Choosing between era, fue, estaba, estuvo, había and hubo
explanations.body: In a story about the past, the imperfect describes the background (what things were like) and the preterite reports events (what happened). Era and estaba set the scene. Fue and estuvo present a completed fact. Había describes what existed, and hubo reports that something took place. Hubo never changes for plural nouns.

rows: state or place in the background

explanations.title: A short history (original summary)
explanations.body: In the nineteenth century, builders laid a railroad across the United States. Thousands of workers took part, and many of them were immigrants from China. The work was hard and dangerous. The last two sections of track met in Utah in 1869. Historians note that for a long time many workers received little recognition.

explanations.body: Certain words point toward the imperfect (background) or the preterite (event). Use them as clues, but always ask: am I describing the scene, or reporting something that happened?

lessons.title: 868. Review: has been doing, had been doing, has been done

explanations.title: Three useful patterns
explanations.body: The perfect continuous (ha estado + gerund / había estado + gerund) says that something has been going on or had been going on for a while. The passive perfect (ha sido / había sido + participle) says that something has been done to a thing. The participle agrees with the thing.

rows: La empresa ha estado buscando una solución.
La empresa había estado perdiendo dinero.
Las medidas habían sido respaldadas por el gobierno.

explanations.title: Notes
explanations.body: Ha habido is impersonal: it stays singular even with plural nouns (ha habido muchos problemas). The gerund of perder is perdiendo, and the gerund of buscar is buscando.

lessons.title: 869. Review: the present perfect subjunctive (haya + participle)

explanations.title: Forming it
explanations.body: The present perfect subjunctive uses haber in the present subjunctive (haya, hayas, haya, hayamos, hayáis, hayan) + a past participle. It describes a completed action when the main clause expresses emotion, doubt, hope or a future condition.

explanations.title: Where you will meet it
explanations.body: Use it after emotion (me alegra que), doubt (dudo que, no creo que), hope (espero que, ojalá) and in future time clauses (cuando, en cuanto, hasta que). In a time clause, the main verb is often in the future or present.

lessons.title: 870. Review: if-sentences about books and rights

explanations.title: Three kinds of if-sentences
explanations.body: Real or likely: si + present, then present or future. Unreal now: si + imperfect subjunctive, then conditional. Unreal past: si + pluperfect subjunctive, then conditional perfect. The examples below discuss a debate. Opinions about how copyright affects creativity differ, so we present it as hypothetical reasoning.

Si la ley no hubiera protegido a los autores, habría habido menos libros.

explanations.title: Reminder
explanations.body: Never use the conditional or the future directly after si in these patterns. Remember that the order of the two clauses can change.

explanations.title: History and debate (brief)
explanations.body: International agreements on intellectual property go back to the nineteenth century. The Paris Convention (1883) deals with industrial property, such as patents and trademarks, and the Berne Convention (1886) deals with literary and artistic works. In the 1990s, the trade agreement known in Spanish as ADPIC (TRIPS in English) set minimum rules for many countries. People disagree about how strict the rules should be: some stress protecting creators, while others stress access to knowledge and culture.

explanations.title: A neutral note

explanations.title: Detroit
explanations.body: In the early 1930s, a car-company leader helped commission a series of murals about local industry for a museum in Detroit. The murals show factory workers, machines and the link between industry and science. Later artists and photographers also documented the changes in that city, which shows how art can serve as a record of different periods.

explanations.title: Quick map
explanations.body: Como si + imperfect subjunctive (or pluperfect subjunctive for an earlier imagined situation). Ojalá + present subjunctive for a possible hope, + imperfect subjunctive for an unlikely present wish, + pluperfect subjunctive for a past regret. Quisiera + infinitive when the subject is the same, quisiera que + imperfect subjunctive when the subjects differ.

explanations.title: Reminder
explanations.body: None of these structures accepts the future or the conditional right after the key word. Como si takes the imperfect or pluperfect subjunctive. Ojalá takes the present, present perfect, imperfect or pluperfect subjunctive, depending on the meaning.

explanations.title: Texto inventado, segunda parte
explanations.body: The fair ends with wishes.

examples.text: El segundo día, un editor explicó que el comercio de libros entre países ha crecido, aunque sigue habiendo desigualdades.
examples.translation: On the second day, an editor explained that the book trade between countries has grown, although inequalities remain.

examples.text: El tercer día, los niños escucharon cuentos.
examples.translation: On the third day, the children listened to stories.

examples.text: Al final, la directora dijo: Ojalá hayamos inspirado a muchos lectores.
examples.translation: At the end, the director said: I hope we have inspired many readers.

examples.text: La directora añadió: Quisiera que la feria se repitiera todos los años.
examples.translation: The director added: I would like the fair to be repeated every year.

exercises.prompt: How long did the fair last?
What was the first day's talk about?
What did the speaker say about easier access to books?
What did the director wish for?
options: That the fair be repeated every year

exercises.prompt: La conferencista habló como si ___ pasado años estudiando el tema.
exercises.promptTranslation: The speaker spoke as if she had spent years studying the subject.

exercises.prompt: Si los autores no ___ protección, muchos no podrían vivir de su trabajo.
exercises.promptTranslation: If authors had no protection, many could not live from their work.

exercises.prompt: Si el acceso a los libros ___ más fácil, habría más lectores.
exercises.promptTranslation: If access to books were easier, there would be more readers.

exercises.prompt: El comercio de libros entre países ___ crecido.
exercises.promptTranslation: The book trade between countries has grown.

exercises.prompt: Ojalá nosotros ___ inspirado ya a muchos lectores.
exercises.promptTranslation: I hope we have inspired many readers.
